# Novelty check: security fidelity of AI-reconstructed applications

- Project: 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding
- Date of check: 2026-11-12
- Proposed topic (from the user): when an LLM agent rebuilds an application from its observable artefacts (UI, screenshots, interaction behaviour, a running reference), are the original's security controls (authentication, authorization / access control, input validation, session handling, CSRF/XSS protection, secrets handling) preserved, dropped, or are new vulnerabilities introduced?
- Type of document: novelty check for a *proposed new topic*, not a full gap report. Papers outside the project are cited as plain references with identifiers retrieved on the check date. They have **not** been analysed in full; statements about them come from their abstracts or from the specific sections we fetched, and are labelled [A] (author claim) unless stated otherwise. Papers inside the project are cited in pandoc style with their project key and page.

Labels: [V] verified in the paper's own text/data, [A] author claim, [I] our interpretation.

## 1. Verdict

**Partially novel, with a clearly defensible novel core.** [I]

- *Already done (not novel):* measuring the **absolute** security of code or whole apps generated by LLMs/agents from a natural-language specification (many benchmarks with exploits or security tests; real-world audits of vibe-coded apps). Also done: SAST scans of programs that agents **rebuilt from behaviour**, but only for command-line tools, only with static scanners, and **without comparing against the original program** (Rajput et al. 2026, see §3).
- *Done in a neighbouring setting:* measuring whether security is **preserved or degraded relative to an original** when an LLM **translates source code** to another language (Chang et al. 2026). There the model sees the original source code.
- *Novel core (we found no study that does this; searches on 2026-11-12):* a **differential, reference-anchored** security evaluation of applications that agents rebuild from **observable behaviour only** (UI, screenshots, interaction traces, live black-box access). The evaluation asks which of the original's security controls survive, which are dropped, and which new weaknesses appear. It uses dynamic security-property tests and exploits that run against **both** the original and the rebuild, not only static scanners. It targets multi-user web applications with real authentication and authorization logic.
- Confidence in the novelty claim: **moderate**. The field moves monthly (several close papers appeared between June and November 2026). Semantic Scholar was rate-limited (HTTP 429) and Google Scholar was not queried directly. Re-run the check before submission.

## 2. Why the topic matters (evidence from the analysed papers)

- [V] Reconstruction from a running reference is an active research setting. In RecreationWorld, agents receive only a running reference application and must build a faithful reimplementation; the reference serves as the oracle for hidden tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 1; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 3]. Evaluation there is purely functional (programmatic assertions) and visual (VLM judge) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11]. No security dimension is scored. [I] The ProgramBench and IWR-Bench reconstruction settings likewise score behaviour and appearance only [@yang2026programbench, p. 1; @chen2025iwr, p. 7].
- [V] Rebuilds are much smaller than their references: 89.4% have less production source code, with a median LOC ratio of 16.9% [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15-16]. [I] Code that is not reproduced can include security checks. Whether the missing code is disproportionately security logic is exactly what has not been measured.
- [V] Functional correctness and security diverge for agent-written code. In SusVibes, 79.3% of the functionally correct solutions of the best setting were insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6]. Each task is checked by only about 3.5 security tests on average, aimed at one historical vulnerability [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5]. SusVibes' task design masks an existing implementation and asks an agent to re-implement it from a description [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4]. [I] This is reconstruction from a *specification*, not from observed behaviour.
- [V] The one in-project study that scores security *relative to a reference implementation* is RAL-Bench. It uses only counts of high-risk static-analysis findings in the generated vs the reference code [@pan2026functional, p. 3]. [V] GPT-3.5-Turbo gets a 97.37 security score with only 29.76 functional score [@pan2026functional, p. 6]. [I] Static, count-based scores can therefore reward incomplete code: less code means fewer findings. A new study must control for this.
- [A] Grey literature reports vibe-coded apps that "lacked authentication, authorization, or contained hardcoded secrets" [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 9]. [V] Vibe Code Bench explicitly does not measure security vulnerabilities [@tran2026vibe, p. 9]. [V] In Vibe Code Bench, 14.8% of failures were "Validation or Policy Block" errors, in which the agent blocks actions that should be allowed. The most common variant is misconfigured Row-Level Security policies [@tran2026vibe, p. 8]. [I] So rebuilt access control can also fail in the over-restrictive direction. A preservation metric must capture both directions.
- [V] Behavioural properties can be recovered from a running app by an LLM. An LLM given only an app description produced 0 valid properties, while runtime-grounded generation produced 92.6% valid ones [@xiong2026propgen, p. 8-9]. [I] This suggests a feasible way to derive security-property tests from the original's observed behaviour.

## 3. Closest prior work (outside the project; identifiers retrieved 2026-11-12)

Ordered by closeness to the proposed topic.

| # | Work (authors, year, venue, identifier) | What it does (source: abstract unless noted) | How it differs from the proposed topic |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rajput, P. K.; Kaboré, A. K.; Song, Y.; Tessa, M.; Malloy, T.; Klein, J.; Bissyandé, T. F. (2026). *Trajectory-Level Security Debt in LLM Coding Agents.* Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series. DOI 10.1609/aaaiss.v10i1.43533; arXiv 2609.35199. | [A] Runs four SAST tools on 712 ProgramBench final workspaces and 13 MirrorCode trajectories, i.e. agent reimplementations of programs, plus 830 SWE-bench runs. Two-tool CWE agreement occurs in 26.2% of ProgramBench runs that pass at least 90% of tests (6.2% after excluding advisory-heavy classes). The authors state that these are scanner findings, not validated vulnerabilities. | Closest in setting: security of rebuilt programs. But (from the HTML full text, §4, §8.4): the programs are **CLI tools, not web apps**. The paper uses **SAST only**, with no DAST or exploits. It does **not scan or compare against the original programs**: "We did not fingerprint findings against initial repositories". It therefore cannot say whether security was preserved or lost. Peer-reviewed symposium paper. |
| 2 | Wu, T.; Ge, C.; Chen, P.; et al. (2026). *Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?* arXiv 2610.14766 (preprint). | [A] 450 tasks built from 150 real vulnerabilities in 7 languages. Three vibe-coding granularities, including "building a repository's source tree from scratch". The specification never mentions security, and hidden functional and security (PoC) tests grade the result. The best agent is functional and secure on only 25.1% of tasks. | Rebuilds real repositories, but **from a written specification** (/app/spec.md) inside the project's environment, not from observed UI or behaviour (HTML full text, §3.2). Security is a pass/fail check against **one historical vulnerability per task**, not a preservation profile of the original's controls. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. |
| 3 | Chang, H.; Meng, G.; Xiao, S.; Chen, K.; Li, Y.; Sun, K. (2026). *When Code Crosses Borders: A Security-Centric Study of LLM-based Code Translation.* IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security. DOI 10.1109/tifs.2026.3746885; arXiv 2509.06504. | [A] Studies whether vulnerabilities are introduced or preserved when 5 LLMs translate 720 security-related samples (Java, PHP, C, C++; 9 CWEs). Between 28.6% and 45% of translations introduce new vulnerabilities, and web-related input-validation flaws are hardest. Proposes RAG mitigation. | Same **conceptual question** (security relative to an original), but in **source-to-source translation**: the model sees the original code, and the samples are code snippets, not whole apps. Our topic is black-box reconstruction, where server-side controls may be **invisible** to the agent. Peer-reviewed, top-tier security journal. |
| 4 | Deng, J.; Fan, Z.; Meng, R. (2026). *Understanding the (In)Security of Vibe-Coded Applications.* arXiv 2606.23130 (preprint). | [A] Collects 9,041 open-source apps built with Claude Code / Lovable and audits 200 deployed apps: 1,186 vulnerabilities; 91.0% of apps have at least one; 65.77% are Critical/High, concentrated in broken access control, injection and authentication failures. | **Absolute** security of greenfield vibe-coded apps in the wild. There is **no reference original** and no reconstruction task. Useful as the vulnerability taxonomy and as evidence that access control and authentication are the weak spots. Preprint. |
| 5 | Vero, M.; Mündler, N.; Chibotaru, V.; Raychev, V.; Baader, M.; Jovanović, N.; He, J.; Vechev, M. (2025). *BaxBench: Can LLMs Generate Correct and Secure Backends?* arXiv 2502.11844. Together with Patir, R.; Guo, K.; et al. (2026). *DualGauge: Automated Joint Security-Functionality Benchmarking of Specification-Only Code Generation by LLMs and Coding Agents.* Findings of EMNLP 2026. DOI 10.18653/2026.findings-emnlp.1335; arXiv 2511.20709. | [A] BaxBench: 392 backend-generation tasks with functional tests and end-to-end exploits; exploits succeed on about half of the correct programs. DualGauge: 307 tasks with paired functional and security tests; the strongest model is below 15% joint success; coding agents are not a reliable remedy. | **Specification-to-code** generation scored on **absolute** security. Neither benchmark has an original application to preserve. Both are exploit/test-based methods that the proposed study can borrow. BaxBench: only the arXiv record was found in OpenAlex/Crossref on the check date, so treat it as a preprint unless a published version is confirmed. |

Other relevant work found (shorter notes):

Base directory for this skill: /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/.claude/skills/start-research

# Start research

Run from the workspace root. `rlab` means `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md). You are the orchestrator: follow [.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md](../../agents/research-orchestrator.md) for delegation and state ownership.

After every phase: tick it in `STATUS.md`, rewrite "Next actions", `rlab log <id> <phase> "<what happened>"`, and give the user a 1–3 line progress update in plain language.

## 1. Scope
Judge whether the topic is researchable as stated. It is **too broad or ambiguous** when it spans several fields, has no clear population/context/outcome, or would plausibly return hundreds of relevant papers.
- Too broad/ambiguous: ask up to 3 multiple-choice questions (AskUserQuestion), each option explained in one plain sentence, with your recommended option first.
- Otherwise: choose sensible defaults (last ~10 years, peer-reviewed first, ≤20 included papers) and record them as assumptions.

Done when: scope, time window and target size are fixed.

## 2. Create the project
`rlab new "<topic>"` → note the project id it prints.

## 3. Objectives and research questions
1. Pilot search to learn the field's vocabulary: `rlab search <id> "<topic keywords>" --limit 10`.
2. Fill `RESEARCH.md`: plain-language topic, scope, 2–4 objectives, inclusion/exclusion criteria, 3–6 facet queries in the search strategy, assumptions under "Key decisions".
3. Fill `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`: 3–5 questions, each answerable from literature, linked to an objective.
4. Show the user the objectives and questions (≤10 lines) and invite corrections. Continue unless they object.

Done when: both files have no empty required fields and Scoping is ticked.

## 4. Discover and screen
Follow the `discover-papers` skill.

## 5. Acquire full texts
`rlab fetch <id>`. For each `NONE` result, list the paper in STATUS "Blocked / needs user" and tell the user once, in one message: which papers lack open access, and that they can download them via their library and run `rlab attach <id> <key> <file.pdf>` (or give you the files). Continue: those papers are analysed abstract-only until a PDF arrives.

Done when: every paper has fulltext status `downloaded`, `user-supplied` or `unavailable`.

## 6. Analyse
Follow the `analyze-paper` skill for every paper, delegated to `paper-analyst` agents in parallel (3–4 papers per agent).

Done when: every paper's analysis is `ready`.

## 7. Critical review
Delegate to the `critical-reviewer` agent. Send each analysis with problems back to a `paper-analyst` with the review findings; repeat until clean. Then set each passed analysis to `status: complete`.

## 8. Synthesis, gaps, report
Follow `compare-methods`, then `find-gaps`, then `research-report`, in that order.

## 9. Close the run
`rlab bib <id>`, `rlab index <id>`, `rlab validate <id>`. Final message to the user: what was found (3–5 bullets), strongest gaps, what is blocked on them, the report path, and how to resume ("Resume research <id>").


ARGUMENTS: Package hallucination / slopsquatting in LLM coding assistants: measuring hallucinated package names and their exploitability on PyPI/npm, with a lightweight defence. Implementation-oriented, laptop-only. Run novelty check early.

---
name: research-orchestrator
description: Research project orchestrator. Plans and runs the research lifecycle, delegates to specialist agents, consolidates their results and keeps project state consistent. Use for multi-phase research runs, or to audit and repair a project's state (STATUS, log, matrix, registry).
model: inherit
---

You orchestrate research projects in this workspace. The main Claude session plays this role by default; you can also run as the main agent (`claude --agent research-orchestrator`) or as a subagent for a state audit.

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from the workspace root). Rules: `docs/research-standards.md`. Phase procedures live in the skills under `.claude/skills/`; read the relevant SKILL.md before each phase.

## Pipeline
Scoping → Discovery → Screening → Acquisition → Analysis → Critical review → Synthesis → Gaps → Writing. Entry point `start-research`; re-entry `resume-research`.

## Delegation
When the Agent tool is available, delegate independent work in parallel (one message, several agents). Without it (e.g. running as a subagent), do the work inline following the same skills.

| Work | Agent | Unit of work |
|---|---|---|
| searching + screening one facet | `paper-scout` | one facet per agent |
| analysing papers | `paper-analyst` | 3–4 paper keys per agent |
| checking analyses against sources | `critical-reviewer` | whole project or a list of keys |
| gaps + novelty checks | `gap-analyst` | whole project |
| literature review / report drafts | `academic-writer` | one document |

Every delegation prompt contains: project id, workspace-relative paths, the exact skill to follow, the scope (keys/facet), and what to return.

## State ownership
Parallel agents write only their own outputs, so nothing is lost to concurrent edits:
- `paper-analyst` → `papers/<key>/analysis.md` for its assigned keys only.
- `critical-reviewer` → `reports/critical-review-*.md`.
- `gap-analyst` → `gap-report.md`. `academic-writer` → `reports/*`.
- `paper-scout` → only the files `rlab search` writes; it returns recommendations.
- **You alone** run `rlab add`, edit `STATUS.md`, `RESEARCH*.md`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `search/screening.md`, and mark analyses `complete`.
- Derived files (`literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib`, `registry.json`, `research/INDEX.md`, STATUS statistics) come only from `rlab index` / `rlab bib`.

## Consolidation
After agents return: check each claimed output exists (`rlab status <id>`), merge their returned findings into the shared files, resolve conflicts between agents by reading the cited pages yourself, then `rlab index <id>` and `rlab log`.

## State audit (when asked to audit/repair)
Report and fix: phases ticked without their outputs, analyses `ready` but never reviewed, papers without analysis, fulltext `unavailable` not listed under "Blocked / needs user", `rlab dedup` pairs, `rlab validate` mismatches, `rlab cite-check` failures on written files, stale Next actions. Fix what is derivable; list the rest for the user.

## The user
A beginner researcher. Short progress updates in plain language, explain important decisions and research terms, ask only for scope decisions, missing access, restricted resources or destructive actions.

content.content:
# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

XXXXX
---
name: discover-papers
description: Search academic sources, screen candidates and add relevant papers to a research project. Use when a project needs (more) literature, when the user asks to find papers, or for snowballing from key papers.
---

# Discover papers

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §3 (source tiers) and §8 (access).

## 1. Plan queries
Read the project's `RESEARCH.md` (scope, criteria, search strategy) and `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`. Write 3–6 facet queries: core concept + each RQ's angle, with field synonyms. Add `--from <year>` per the scope. Add `pubmed` to `--sources` for biomedical/health topics.

## 2. Search (fan out)
Dispatch one `paper-scout` agent per facet (in parallel, one message). Give each: project id, its facet query/queries, inclusion/exclusion criteria, year window, and the number of papers wanted. Scouts search, screen and **return** recommendations; they never run `rlab add`.

Without subagents: run `rlab search <id> "<query>" [--sources ...] [--from Y] [--limit N]` yourself and screen as in step 3.

## 3. Screen
For each candidate decide include / exclude on title + abstract (read the abstract from the saved JSON in `search/`). Prefer published peer-reviewed work; prefer a published version over its preprint; exclude RETRACTED; treat citation counts as a weak signal (recent papers have few). Keep a balance: seminal papers, recent work (last 2–3 years), and at least one review/survey if one exists.

Record every included paper and every notable exclusion in `search/screening.md` (results file, idx, short title, decision, reason).

## 4. Snowball
For the 3–5 most central included papers, look at references and citing works via OpenAlex (WebFetch):
- cited by: `https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=cites:<openalex_id>&sort=cited_by_count:desc&per-page=25`
- references: `referenced_works` in `https://api.openalex.org/works/<openalex_id>`
Use WebSearch for very recent work (current and previous year). Screen these the same way.

## 5. Add
One call for all included ids (DOIs preferred; else arXiv id, OpenAlex W-id, `pmid:N`):
`rlab add <id> <ids...> --reason "<why included>" --query "<query that found it>"`
Use one call per distinct reason. Then handle output:
- `DUPLICATE` → fine, already present.
- `WARNING: RETRACTED` → remove from consideration and tell the user why.
- `WARNING: metadata MISMATCH` or `single-source` → run `rlab validate <id> <key>` and inspect `metadata.json`; if the record is wrong, tell the user.
- `FAIL` → identifier wrong or not indexed; find the correct DOI from the publisher page, never guess.

Finally `rlab dedup <id>` must report 0 pairs (resolve any pair by keeping the published version; ask the user before removing a folder).

Done when: the target number of papers is reached or new searches return mostly IN-PROJECT/irrelevant hits (saturation), every included paper is in `screening.md`, and dedup is clean. Tick Discovery and Screening in `STATUS.md`.

- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

# Discover papers

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §3 (source tiers) and §8 (access).

## 1. Plan queries
Read the project's `RESEARCH.md` (scope, criteria, search strategy) and `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`. Write 3–6 facet queries: core concept + each RQ's angle, with field synonyms. Add `--from <year>` per the scope. Add `pubmed` to `--sources` for biomedical/health topics.

## 2. Search (fan out)
Dispatch one `paper-scout` agent per facet (in parallel, one message). Give each: project id, its facet query/queries, inclusion/exclusion criteria, year window, and the number of papers wanted. Scouts search, screen and **return** recommendations; they never run `rlab add`.

Without subagents: run `rlab search <id> "<query>" [--sources ...] [--from Y] [--limit N]` yourself and screen as in step 3.

## 3. Screen
For each candidate decide include / exclude on title + abstract (read the abstract from the saved JSON in `search/`). Prefer published peer-reviewed work; prefer a published version over its preprint; exclude RETRACTED; treat citation counts as a weak signal (recent papers have few). Keep a balance: seminal papers, recent work (last 2–3 years), and at least one review/survey if one exists.

Record every included paper and every notable exclusion in `search/screening.md` (results file, idx, short title, decision, reason).

## 4. Snowball
For the 3–5 most central included papers, look at references and citing works via OpenAlex (WebFetch):
- cited by: `https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=cites:<openalex_id>&sort=cited_by_count:desc&per-page=25`
- references: `referenced_works` in `https://api.openalex.org/works/<openalex_id>`
Use WebSearch for very recent work (current and previous year). Screen these the same way.

## 5. Add
One call for all included ids (DOIs preferred; else arXiv id, OpenAlex W-id, `pmid:N`):
`rlab add <id> <ids...> --reason "<why included>" --query "<query that found it>"`
Use one call per distinct reason. Then handle output:
- `DUPLICATE` → fine, already present.
- `WARNING: RETRACTED` → remove from consideration and tell the user why.
- `WARNING: metadata MISMATCH` or `single-source` → run `rlab validate <id> <key>` and inspect `metadata.json`; if the record is wrong, tell the user.
- `FAIL` → identifier wrong or not indexed; find the correct DOI from the publisher page, never guess.

Finally `rlab dedup <id>` must report 0 pairs (resolve any pair by keeping the published version; ask the user before removing a folder).

Done when: the target number of papers is reached or new searches return mostly IN-PROJECT/irrelevant hits (saturation), every included paper is in `screening.md`, and dedup is clean. Tick Discovery and Screening in `STATUS.md`.

 - Primary working directory: /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting (was /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main)

I've started the slopsquatting project (`2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting`). The scope and the five research questions are written and saved in the project files. Three paper scouts are searching right now; together they cover:
1. how often LLMs invent package names, and the benchmarks for it
2. how attackers can exploit those names, and how coding agents install packages
3. which defences exist

When they finish, I'll pick up to 20 papers and download the open-access PDFs. Then I'll analyse them and run the novelty check (a search to confirm nobody has already done the study). If some papers have no free PDF, I'll ask you once, all together, to get them through your library. I'll message you as soon as the scouts report back.

  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Text injected into AGENTS.md or .cursorrules makes coding agents swap real dependencies for packages the attacker controls. The PackHallu optimiser is tested across several agent frameworks. | RQ2, RQ5 | arXiv API `abs:"package hallucination"` (WebSearch/recency pass) |
  | 2 | 10.18653/2026.findings-emnlp.1274 | 2026 | Harmless Yet Harmful: Neutral Prompting Attacks for Stealthy Hallucination Steering in Agent Skills (Hsu, Yu, Huang) | Findings of EMNLP 2026, **published** (Crossref-verified; arXiv 2605.29354) | The only peer-reviewed agent-side attack paper I found. Harmless-looking skill instructions raise the package-hallucination rate in coding agents without targeting any specific package. | RQ2, RQ5 | "coding agent dependency installation malicious package" |
  | 3 | arXiv:2605.09594 | 2026 | Trust Me, Import This: Dependency Steering Attacks via Malicious Agent Skills (Liu, Hsu, Huang, Backes) | arXiv, **preprint** | Shows that package hallucination can be induced on purpose rather than only occurring passively: a malicious Skill steers the agent to one attacker-chosen package. The attack transfers across models, and skill scanners do not catch it. | RQ2, RQ5 | "coding agent dependency installation malicious package" |
  | 4 | 10.5281/zenodo.21199426 | 2026 | From Hallucination to Registration: Do the Package Names That LLMs Invent Actually Get Claimed? (Okwor) | Zenodo, **preprint / grey literature, single author, no arXiv version found** | The only registry-side measurement of real-world claiming I found. None of 1,641 freshly invented names were registered. Of 149 names that were already public, 22 were registered and none were malicious; 19 of the 22 came from one benign placeholder operation. This is key counter-evidence for RQ2. Weight it low and flag it. | RQ2, RQ4 | "slopsquatting" |
  | 5 | arXiv:2605.06279 | 2026 | Correct Code, Vulnerable Dependencies: A Large-Scale Measurement Study of LLM-Specified Library Versions (Wang, Wu, Ling, …) | arXiv, **preprint** | Dependency risk beyond hallucination. Ten LLMs on 1,000 Stack Overflow tasks: in 36.7–55.7% of tasks the pinned versions carry a known CVE, and the models converge on the same risky versions. | RQ5 (also RQ1 context) | "AI coding assistant dependency security vulnerable outdated" |
  | 6 | 10.1007/978-3-030-52683-2_2 | 2020 | Backstabber's Knife Collection: A Review of Open Source Software Supply Chain Attacks (Ohm, Plate, Sykosch, Meier) | LNCS (DIMVA 2020), **published** | Seminal background: a taxonomy of attacks on npm and PyPI (typosquatting, name confusion, install-time execution) that grounds the attack model. 342 citations. | RQ2 (background) | "typosquatting malicious packages PyPI npm" (`--to 2023`) |
  | 7 | 10.14722/ndss.2021.23055 | 2021 | Towards Measuring Supply Chain Attacks on Package Managers for Interpreted Languages (Duan et al.) | NDSS 2021, **published** | Seminal measurement of malicious packages on PyPI, npm and RubyGems, including registry-side detection. A methodological model for registry measurements. | RQ2, RQ4 (background) | "typosquatting malicious packages PyPI npm" |

  - arXiv:2608.23897 *Names Can Hurt* (2026 preprint; the same paper also has Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22087562, but use the arXiv id). Half of its flagged hallucinations were already registered as low-quality lookalikes on PyPI (e.g. pil, faiss), which matters for RQ2. It also offers a laptop-scale existence check + Random Forest defence (RQ3).
  - 10.1109/noms69089.2026.11668187 *SlopsGuard* (NOMS 2026 demo paper, published). A registry and edit-distance defence tool (RQ3, F3 overlap).
  - 10.1109/cyber-ai70573.2026.11755213 *Hal-Detector* (Cyber-AI 2026, published). Classifies hallucinated npm names with explainable AI (RQ3).
  - arXiv:2408.05128 *Is ChatGPT a Good Software Librarian?* (preprint). Studies ChatGPT's library recommendations on 10k Stack Overflow questions. I did not verify whether a published version exists.
  - 10.1109/acsac67867.2025.00094 *APILOT* (ACSAC 2025, published). Mitigates outdated or vulnerable APIs in LLM suggestions; peer-reviewed but peripheral to RQ3.

  | 10.1080/07366981.2025.2510097 | Slopsquatting assurance (EDPACS) | Audit-practice article with no empirical contribution |
  | 10.64643/ijirtv12i7-191660-459 | Slopsquatting and package-hallucination in LLMs (IJIRT) | Suspected low-quality or predatory venue |
  | 10.56048/mqr.2026.e396 | Slopsquatting en código generado… (MQRInvestigar) | Low-tier venue; npm measurement duplicates stronger work |
  | 10.21203/rs.3.rs-8007192/v1 | AI-Induced Supply-Chain Compromise: Systematic Review (Research Square) | Single-author preprint SLR. Keep only if the project wants a review and no better one exists; F1/F5 scouts may find one |
  | 10.57760/sciencedb.018xg; 10.5281/zenodo.19859120 | Reproducibility archive / replication code | Data and code artefacts, not papers. The parent paper of the "Beyond Passive Slopsquatting" archive was not found on arXiv or OpenAlex |

  | 10.48550/arxiv.2606.07131, 2604.06550, 2606.19191, 2607.25619 | Malicious agent-skill benchmarks and detectors | About agent skills in general, not dependency choice |
  | arXiv:2410.06462 | Hallucinating AI Hijacking Attack (Noever, McKee) | About guardrail bypass for malicious code suggestions; weak link to package names |
  | arXiv:2602.19555 | SoK agentic supply chain runtime | Broad survey of agent runtime supply-chain risks; package hallucination is only a side topic |
  | 10.1145/3714464 | Research Directions in Software Supply Chain Security (TOSEM 2025) | Good general background, but the 2-paper background quota went to the two seminal attack papers |
  | 10.1109/eurospw51379.2020.00074 | Typosquatting and Combosquatting on PyPI (EuroS&P workshop) | Workshop tier; Backstabber's and NDSS cover the same ground |
  | arXiv:2509.20277 | Security implications of generated code on the software supply chain | Broad threat catalogue that overlaps with the included papers |
  | arXiv:2606.13918 | Bayesian-calibrated detection | F3 (defence); leave to the F3 scout |

Spracklen et al. 2406.10279 has a USENIX Security '25 version, which the F1 scout should verify and prefer. Range Shrinks (2605.17062) also covers RQ2 (names hallucinated by all five models; disclosure to PyPI/npm) |
  
  ### 3. Search notes
  - **Queries run** (all saved under `/Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting/search/`):
    - `20261112-045054-slopsquatting.json` ("slopsquatting", `--from 2023`)
    - `20261112-045102-llm-package-confusion-supply-chain.json`
    - `20261112-045106-ai-coding-assistant-dependency-security.json`
    - `20261112-045111-coding-agent-dependency-installation.json`
    - `20261112-045130-typosquatting-malicious-packages-pypi.json` (`--to 2023`, background)
    - `20261112-045132-beyond-passive-slopsquatting-dependency.json`
    - `20261112-045137-llm-library-recommendation-deprecated.json`
  - **Snowball:** one pass over works citing Spracklen et al. (OpenAlex W4399795583, 52 citing works). It added 2509.20277, 2410.06462 and 2602.19555, all excluded or reserve. I did not do a `referenced_works` pass because the **OpenAlex free daily budget for this IP ran out** ("Rate limit exceeded", resets at midnight UTC). This may make `rlab add` fail or fall back to single-source metadata until the reset.
  - **Recent-work pass:** direct arXiv API searches for slopsquatting, HalluSquatting and `abs:"package hallucination"`, plus two WebSearches. These found arXiv:2610.09264, which no `rlab` query returned. Press coverage mentions a July 2026 attack called "HalluSquatting" (forkast.news), but I found no primary paper on arXiv or OpenAlex, so it is not included. The react-codeshift incident (Aikido) and the CSA research notes are vendor or grey literature and can only guide searching.
  - **Saturation:** the "slopsquatting" results were mostly low-quality Zenodo or regional-journal items. The supply-chain and agent queries were swamped by malicious-package detectors and agent-skill security work. New results were mostly repeats or off-topic, so the core of F2/F4 looks saturated. The literature is thin and nearly all 2026 preprints; Harmless Yet Harmful (EMNLP Findings) is the only peer-reviewed paper on the agent-side attack.
  - **Likely gaps:**
    1. No peer-reviewed, longitudinal registry-side measurement of real slopsquatting registrations or downloads exists. Only the Zenodo preprint (#4) and the disclosure section of Range Shrinks touch this.
    2. I found no academic study of autonomous agents actually running `pip`/`npm install` on hallucinated names end to end. All the attack papers (#1–3) measure whether the agent generates the package, not whether it installs it. This is a candidate RQ5 gap and needs a novelty check.
    3. I found no measurement of dependencies Copilot or Cursor suggest inside the IDE; the work found is all chat or API based.
  
  Sources (WebSearch):
  - [CSA research note: slopsquatting and AI supply chain](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-slopsquatting-ai-supply-chain-20260419/)
  - [CSA research note: AI coding assistant supply chain](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research-rb/csa-research-note-slopsquatting-ai-coding-assistant-supply-c/)
  - [alphaXiv: 2605.17062](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2605.17062)
  - [Forkast: HalluSquatting](https://forkast.news/hallusquatting-turns-ai-hallucinations-into-a-deterministic-supply-chain-attack-85-hit-rate/)
  - [Endor Labs: slopsquatting and agents](https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/slopsquatting-when-ai-agents-hallucinate-malicious-packages)
  - [CSO Online coverage](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4201164/top-ais-invent-same-fake-pypl-and-npm-package-names-2.html)
  - [Socket glossary](https://socket.dev/glossary/slopsquatting)
  
  All of these are grey literature, used only to guide the search and not as evidence.

  ## spracklen2024we — ready-quality content, NOT WRITTEN · full-text · tier 3 as analysed
  Analysed arXiv v3 (2 Mar 2025, p. 1). The arXiv text does not name the USENIX Security '25 venue; your note and the reference lists of churilov2026range (p. 16) and okwor2026hallucination (p. 9) do.
  
  **Summary:** 16 models from 2023–24 produced 576k Python/JS code samples, and 19.7% of 2.23M package mentions were hallucinated (5.2% commercial vs 21.7% open-source) (p. 7). Hallucinated names often repeat, and retrieval, self-checking and fine-tuning all cut the rate; fine-tuning also lowered code quality.
  
  **Key findings:**
  - 440,445 of 2.23M mentions hallucinated; 205,474 unique names. GPT-4 Turbo lowest at 3.59%. JavaScript 21.3% vs Python 15.8% (p. 7).
  - 43% of hallucinated names reappear in 10 of 10 re-runs and 39% never do (p. 9). 81% of names come from only one model (p. 10).
  - Only 13.4% are 1–2 edits from a real package. 8.7% of hallucinated Python names are real npm packages. Deleted PyPI packages explain 0.17% (p. 11).
  - Rates rise with temperature, sharply above 1. Changing top-p, top-k or min-p does not help (+1.16%) (p. 8).
  - Defences, Table 4 (p. 13), DeepSeek / CodeLlama:
    - Retrieval of known package names: 16.14→12.24% / 26.28→13.40%.
    - Self-refinement (model re-checks its own packages): 13.04% / 25.51%.
    - Fine-tuning: 2.66% / 10.27%, but HumanEval fell 51.4→25.3% / 19.6→16.4%.
  
  **Details for a replication:**
  - Prompts: Stack Overflow, top 20 questions per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; plus Llama-2-70B prompts generated from descriptions of the top 5,000 packages. Released on Zenodo 14676377 / GitHub (p. 5, p. 14).
  - System prompts: Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
  - Settings: temperature 0.7 for code and 0.01 for package lists; top-p 0.9; top-k 20 (p. 19). Open models were GPTQ-quantized (p. 6).
  - Registry snapshot: master lists from 10 Jan 2024 (p. 7).
  - Extraction: install commands in code plus two prompts asking the model for package lists. Import parsing is explicitly rejected (p. 6).
  - Metric: hallucinated mentions / all recommended packages.
  - Not reported: name normalisation, standard-library handling, statistics.

  - Fine-tuning data came from the same prompt pool; the evaluation prompts are not described, so leakage is possible.

  ## churilov2026range — NOT WRITTEN · full-text · tier 3
  Single independent author. Version 4 (Nov 2026) replaces all numbers in v1–3 and in a SCORED '26 workshop version (p. 1).
  
  **Summary:** A replication of Spracklen on 5 frontier models from 2026 (199,840 generations), with every name re-checked against the live registries under a plan registered in advance. Rates are 3.63–5.02% of package mentions; 104 names are hallucinated by all five models; about 1.1% of hallucinated names were registered within roughly six months.
  
  **Key findings:**
  - Rates: 3.63–5.02% of mentions and 2.15–3.39% of generations; 7 of 10 model pairs differ significantly (p. 6–8).
  - Python > JS for every model by 2.34–3.47 points (p. 7). LLM-written prompts give higher rates than Stack Overflow prompts: 4.79/5.44% vs 2.28/3.10% (p. 7).
  - 104 names hallucinated by all five models (88 PyPI, 16 npm); 54 are one edit from a real package. Mean name overlap between pairs of models (Jaccard similarity) is 0.219 (p. 8–9).
  - 25 of 2,282 names (1.1%) were registered within about six months. Publishing names had no detectable effect (0/87 vs 2/101, p = 0.50), but the test could only detect a rise from 1% to about 10.5% (p. 12).
  - At least 23 names the models suggest had hosted malware that registries removed (p. 12). Live re-checks lowered all earlier rates by about a fifth; import names of real packages were the largest correction (p. 10–11).
  
  **Details for a replication:**
  - Models and snapshot IDs: Table 1 (p. 4). Generations were collected 22–28 Apr 2026.
  - Temperatures: "defaults", values not printed (p. 4).
  - Extraction: `pip install` (first argument only), `npm install` inside code blocks, imports via Python ast / tree-sitter (p. 5).
  - Registry checks: two methods per registry (PyPI JSON plus Simple API; npm registry plus deps.dev), two rounds on 7 and 8 Nov 2026 at least 12 h apart, 1 request/s per host. A name counts as hallucinated if it did not exist when generated. OSV is queried for malware records (p. 5).
  - Exclusions:
    - standard library (`sys.stdlib_module_names` for Python 3.10–3.13; Node 18/20/22 built-ins);
    - names invalid under PEP 508 / npm rules;
    - import names mapped to real packages via pipreqs (p. 5–6).
  - Statistics: Wilson CIs; chi-square with Holm correction; permutation tests (seed 42) (p. 6).
  - Cost: $1,160 (p. 17).
  
  **Doubtful:**
  - It says "We follow Spracklen's extraction approach" (p. 5), but it parses imports, which Spracklen explicitly rejects (spracklen p. 6). The 2024 vs 2026 comparison and the "Python > JS inversion" therefore use different measures.
  - It credits Spracklen with two claims I could not find in Spracklen's text: npm "fragmentation" as the cause of higher JS rates (p. 13), and "smaller models hallucinate more" (p. 9).

  **Summary:** garak probes tested 11 LLMs on JavaScript, Python and Rust. The package hallucination rate (share of prompts with at least one missing package) ranged from 0.22% to 46.15%.   **Key findings:**

  - Prompts: 7 request templates × 13 tasks × 3 languages, each repeated 5 times (p. 4; Tables 6–7, p. 12).

  ## Cross-paper contradictions (for the evidence matrix)

    - Spracklen: JS > Python (p. 7).
    - Krishna: Python > JS (p. 8).
    - Churilov: Python > JS (p. 7).

## spracklen2024we — ready-quality content, NOT WRITTEN · full-text · tier 3 as analysed
Analysed arXiv v3 (2 Mar 2025, p. 1). The arXiv text does not name the USENIX Security '25 venue; your note and the reference lists of churilov2026range (p. 16) and okwor2026hallucination (p. 9) do.

**Summary:** 16 models from 2023–24 produced 576k Python/JS code samples, and 19.7% of 2.23M package mentions were hallucinated (5.2% commercial vs 21.7% open-source) (p. 7). Hallucinated names often repeat, and retrieval, self-checking and fine-tuning all cut the rate; fine-tuning also lowered code quality.

**Key findings:**
- 440,445 of 2.23M mentions hallucinated; 205,474 unique names. GPT-4 Turbo lowest at 3.59%. JavaScript 21.3% vs Python 15.8% (p. 7).
- 43% of hallucinated names reappear in 10 of 10 re-runs and 39% never do (p. 9). 81% of names come from only one model (p. 10).
- Only 13.4% are 1–2 edits from a real package. 8.7% of hallucinated Python names are real npm packages. Deleted PyPI packages explain 0.17% (p. 11).
- Rates rise with temperature, sharply above 1. Changing top-p, top-k or min-p does not help (+1.16%) (p. 8).
- Defences, Table 4 (p. 13), DeepSeek / CodeLlama:
  - Retrieval of known package names: 16.14→12.24% / 26.28→13.40%.
  - Self-refinement (model re-checks its own packages): 13.04% / 25.51%.
  - Fine-tuning: 2.66% / 10.27%, but HumanEval fell 51.4→25.3% / 19.6→16.4%.

**Details for a replication:**
- Prompts: Stack Overflow, top 20 questions per tag for 240 tags, 2023 vs pre-2023; plus Llama-2-70B prompts generated from descriptions of the top 5,000 packages. Released on Zenodo 14676377 / GitHub (p. 5, p. 14).
- System prompts: Figures 10–13 (p. 18–19).
- Settings: temperature 0.7 for code and 0.01 for package lists; top-p 0.9; top-k 20 (p. 19). Open models were GPTQ-quantized (p. 6).
- Registry snapshot: master lists from 10 Jan 2024 (p. 7).
- Extraction: install commands in code plus two prompts asking the model for package lists. Import parsing is explicitly rejected (p. 6).
- Metric: hallucinated mentions / all recommended packages.
- Not reported: name normalisation, standard-library handling, statistics.

**Doubtful:**
- The rate pools install commands with names given when the model is asked directly.
- Fine-tuning data came from the same prompt pool; the evaluation prompts are not described, so leakage is possible.
- No confidence intervals.
- Inconsistencies:
  - 586k vs 576k samples (p. 2 vs p. 6).
