- Correction: "Of the 2,000 extra generations, 11 produced names absent from the snapshot but live (p. 7). The author calls this 'essentially uninformative' given the few-day window (p. 7)."

3.5 Missing RQ2-relevant content.
- Paper, p. 2: Lanyado's registered hallucinated name `huggingface-cli` drew more than 30,000 downloads in three months; a hallucinated npm name spread to 237 GitHub repositories before a researcher defensively claimed it.
- Add as "[A] secondary claims citing grey sources [4, 5] (p. 2); not verified by this paper". Our RQ2 asks directly about real-world slopsquatting.

3.6 §5 Code availability.
- Current text: "Not yet available (p. 8)".
- Paper, p. 8: "will be deposited". We did not check whether it has been.
- Correction: "[A] promised (p. 8); we did not check whether the deposit exists."

3.7 Header tier.
- The analysis says tier 4 (grey literature). The paper self-labels "Preprint, July 2026" (p. 1). Under standards §3 that is tier 3, with a company affiliation.
- Either tier is defensible. State the reason (single author, company-affiliated, Zenodo self-deposit, no peer review) so the tier choice is not arbitrary.

======================================================================
4. krishna2025importing: PASS-WITH-MINOR-FIXES
Number check: 14 values grepped (Table 3 cells, 14.73/23.14/24.74, σ 16.03/14.37/8.43, r = −0.542 / p = 0.00114, −0.593 / 0.00028, −0.7887, −0.2919, Table 4 means, Table 2 counts, Mamba 21.03 vs Llama-8B 15.24, "15 billion", µ = 26.90%). All are correct. We recomputed the Python mean from Table 3: 254.51 / 11 = 23.14.

4.1 §10 External.
- Current text: "[V] This is the only study in our set that covers Rust and crates.io (p. 4)".
- This is false: zheng2026when is Rust-only, dasu2026refusing has nonexistent-crate prompts, and spracklen2024we checks Cargo for cross-language names (p. 11).
- Correction: "[V] Covers Rust/crates.io alongside JS and Python (p. 4). [I] Within the project, Rust is also covered by [@zheng2026when] and [@dasu2026refusing]."

4.2 §4 Sample size: the estimate can be confirmed from the data.
- The smallest PHR, 0.22%, equals 1/455; the largest, 46.15%, equals 210/455 (Table 3, p. 4). This fits 7 stubs × 13 tasks × 5 repeats = 455 prompts per model-language cell.
- Add: "[I] Table 3 values are multiples of 1/455, which supports N = 455 per model-language cell. Nemotron's 0.22% is a single prompt."

4.3 §6 / §9 statistics: a missing threat.
- Table 1 (p. 3): GPT-4o's size, "200B*", is "an approximation, from Abacha et al. (2024)" (a medical-benchmark paper). GPT-4o is the extreme x-value in the size correlation.
- Add: "[I] The size correlation depends on an unverified 200B estimate for GPT-4o (Table 1 footnote, p. 3)."

4.4 §7 finding 3, "Best models".
- Dracarys has the lowest Python PHR, 2.42% (Table 3, p. 4; text p. 5), lower than GPT-4o (3.52%) and Nemotron (4.84%).
- Add: "Lowest Python: Dracarys 2.42%."

======================================================================
5. zhao2025hfuzzer: PASS-WITH-MINOR-FIXES
Provenance: published at ASE 2025 (verified). Number check: 13 values grepped (2.60×, 4.89×, 5.13×, 0.26–0.66%, 5.68/7.10/9.82/16.47%, 3.02×, 190/176, 17, 2.36×/2.46×, ablation 2.06/1.39/1.27 and 4.40/1.25/1.26, 46/34/12, k-parameters). All are on pp. 1–9.

5.1 §5 and §9 bullet 1.
- Current text: "the registry query date is not reported".
- Paper: reference [13] "Pypi ... last accessed Mar. 2025" (p. 12).
- Correction: "Registry query date not stated; PyPI 'last accessed Mar. 2025' in reference [13] (p. 12) is the best proxy."

5.2 §13 RQ4 row.
- Current text: "34 of 46 ... arise at the install-command stage with correct imports; import-regex extraction misses them" [V].
- The "misses them" part is the authors' hypothesis (p. 9). It is also not strictly true: an import-regex extractor without import→package mapping would extract `pywt` too (same string), for a different reason.
- Correction: split the row. "[V] 34 of 46 are package errors with correct imports (p. 9)" and "[A] import-based extraction overlooks install-stage hallucinations (p. 9)".

5.3 §13 RQ3 row.
- Mixes [V] data with our proposal ("comment-aware filtering is a possible cheap check").
- Correction: keep "[V] 12 cases (p. 9)" and move the suggestion to §11 as [I].

5.4 §7 finding 12.
- Current text: "temperature shows no clear trend".
- Paper, p. 10: the temperature tested is that of the tester model, on two combinations only.
- Correction: "tester-model temperature (two combinations) shows no clear trend (p. 10)."

5.5 §3: β is printed as "0.51" in the text layer (p. 4); this is a footnote marker attached to 0.5. The analysis has 0.5, which is correct. No change; noted for anyone re-quoting.

======================================================================
6. haque2025secure: PASS-WITH-MINOR-FIXES
Number check: all Table 1 cells cited (PHR and VPR, including the Paraphrase VPR column 15.57→8.22 and 12.30→9.57), Table 2 counts and the p. 7 discussion figures. All are correct. Table 2's 1.5B 4-bit SO row sums to 7,550 with 4,751 hallucinated = 62.93%, consistent with Table 1.

6.1 §7 finding 6 and the §13 RQ2 row.
- Current text: "[V] Hallucinated strings are mostly URL-like Go module paths".
- Paper, p. 6: "the LLM generated package strings mostly in the url category". That refers to all generated strings, and "Across all models" cannot be checked because only one table (1.5B 4-bit) is printed. In that table, URL categories account for 2,418 of 4,751 hallucinated SO strings (51%); file paths (1,372) and "other" (961) make up 49% (Table 2, p. 8).
- Correction: "[A] Generated strings are mostly URLs, mainly github.com/golang.org (p. 6). [V] In the only table shown (1.5B 4-bit, SO), 2,418 of 4,751 (51%) hallucinated strings are URLs and 2,333 (49%) are file paths or free-form strings (Table 2, p. 8)."

6.2 §9 bullet 3: strengthen with the number above.
- Add: "[I] About half of 'hallucinated packages' in the one cell shown are not installable module paths, so PHR overstates squattable names."

6.3 §3: "One generation pass per prompt is implied" has no label. Mark it [I].

======================================================================
7. zheng2026when: PASS-WITH-MINOR-FIXES
Number check: 18 values grepped (22.23%, 10,779/48,494, 16,764, 16.18/26.90, 1.66, 23.34/20.79/25.23, Table 2 range 18.46–21.92, F-tests, 45.47%, "over half", 1,086/828, Jaccard 0.44/0.16, 55.05/25.42%, 5,647/13,332, 3.42/40.78/86.48/2.36/32.96%, 38.9%, Table 4 deltas). All are correct. The p. 1 quote is verified (lines 47–48).

7.1 Header venue.
- Current text: "An acceptance at Internetware 2026 was reported to us as an author claim".
- This is unsourced: the PDF does not mention it, and metadata says arXiv.
- Correction: delete it, or move it to Analyst notes as "unverified venue claim from [source]; not in PDF or metadata". If a published version exists, resolve it with `rlab add`.

7.2 §5: name normalisation not addressed.
- Cargo treats `-` and `_` as equivalent (a crate is published as `tokio-util` and referenced as `tokio_util`). The paper does not report how source identifiers were matched to crates.io names. It does report a hyphen-omission pattern (32.96%, p. 7).
- Add: "Hyphen/underscore normalisation between source identifiers and crates.io names: not reported. [I] Without it, hyphenated crates would be counted as hallucinations; with it, the hyphen-omission finding needs re-checking."

7.3 §7 finding 7 [A] contrast with prior work.
- Units differ. Zheng's 40.78% / 86.48% are occurrence-weighted ("hallucination occurrences", p. 7). Spracklen's 13.4% / 48.6% are over 76,489 unique Python names ([@spracklen2024we, p. 11]).
- Add: "[I] Not directly comparable: occurrence-weighted (Rust, non-module) vs unique names (Python)."

7.4 §5: the main run used the largest open sizes from Ollama (p. 5), including DeepSeek-Coder-V2 236B. The "to be checked" quantization caveat applies to all open models in RQ1 too, not only the size sweep. Extend §9 bullet 6 accordingly.

======================================================================
8. dasu2026refusing: PASS-WITH-MINOR-FIXES
Number check: 20 values grepped (54/31/15%, 1/1,547, HR range 0.23–0.90, Table IV and Table V cells, Spearman values, 100% for DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss 120B, 94/87/76/63/63/33% and 87/84/68/50/50/15%, 14% vs 94%, B1–B4 shares, 47/43/18%, 0.64 vs 0.43, CI 8–34, 34% vs 15%, 33/270, 11, pywfm, 28/23/5, judge κ values, 12 npm + 10 crate prompts on p. 9). All are correct.

8.1 §13 RQ2 row "33 of 270 prompts fool at least 16 of 17 models".
- Mapping problem: in the plausible-entity family the package name is planted by the prompt (p. 3; p. 10 "we plant a name"). Cross-model "repetition" of that name is trivially the planted name, so this is not evidence that invented names are predictable.
- Correction: re-map the row to RQ1/RQ4 (prompt-driven acceptance), or add "[I] names are supplied by the prompt; not evidence of spontaneous cross-model name repetition".

8.2 §13 RQ3 row "18% of plausible-entity hallucinations are 'factual' ... and would evade registry checks" [V].
- Paper, p. 7: these responses use "only real packages and APIs"; "no registry check will notice" is the authors' wording.
- [I] These responses install no nonexistent package, so they carry no slopsquatting risk. Using them as evidence against registry-check defences is misleading for our RQ3.
- Correction: "[V] 18% are factual (p. 7). [A] 'no registry check will notice' (p. 7). [I] These responses install no fictitious package, so they do not bear on slopsquatting defences."

8.3 §13 RQ2 row "Misspelled real package names are caught 86% of the time".
- Paper, p. 8: a misspelled name is "fabricated on 14% of prompts". The remaining 86% are correct (typo fixed) or refusals (p. 4 rule).
- Correction: "fabricated on 14% (vs 94% for fictional names); the rest are corrected or refused (p. 4, p. 8)."

8.4 §7 finding 3.
- Add the per-group counts: small = 4 models, mid = 8, large = 5 (Table V, p. 6).
- Add: "[I] The npm+crates subset has 22 prompts per model, so 1.00 / 0.90 / 0.85 rest on 88 / 176 / 110 responses."

======================================================================
9. zhang2025llm: PASS-WITH-MINOR-FIXES
Number check: taxonomy shares (43.53 = 36.66 + 6.86; 31.91 = 8.82 + 2.68 + 20.41; 24.56 = 0.94 + 11.26 + 12.36), Table I Pass@1, 1,380 seed snippets and temperature 0.6. All are correct (pp. 3–9).

9.1 Venue (the caller's premise is not supported).
- The caller wrote "PACMSE/FSE 2025". Three project papers cite this work as Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering vol. 2, issue ISSTA (2025), pp. 481–503:
  - [@zheng2026when, p. 11];
  - [@dasu2026refusing, p. 11] ("in ISSTA, 2025");
  - liu2026mitigating fulltext line 766–767.
- The analysis's ISSTA attribution is the evidenced one. Do not change it to FSE unless the DOI landing page says otherwise.
- Keep the §9 bullet. Add the full citation "PACMSE 2(ISSTA): 481–503" and the liu2026mitigating citation.

9.2 Header / source version.
- The analysed PDF is arXiv v2 (5 authors). metadata.oa_pdf_url points to a legal OA ACM DL copy of the published version (9 authors).
- Standards §3 prefer the published version.
- Fix: put "published version available OA (metadata oa_pdf_url); not yet analysed" in STATUS/Next actions. Attaching it would replace paper.pdf, which needs the user's explicit permission under §9.

9.3 §7 finding 2 and the §13 RQ1 row.
- `_lfu_cache` is described as the "package-existence case" (pp. 6–7).
- [I] A leading underscore is not a valid PyPI distribution name under PEP 508 (names must start with a letter or digit). The example is more likely a missing project-internal module than an invented registry name.
- Add: "[I] `_lfu_cache` cannot be registered on PyPI as written, so it is not a slopsquatting target; Environment Conflicts (0.94%) are an upper bound on invented-package cases, if anything."

======================================================================
CROSS-PAPER NOTES FOR THE EVIDENCE MATRIX
(evidence-matrix.md is currently empty, 13 lines.)

A. Rate units: never pool or rank these figures across papers.
- spracklen2024we: mention-level (hallucinated names / all names). It pools H1 install commands in code with H2/H3 answers the model gives when asked directly. Only 19.7% is pooled. 5.2% / 21.7% / 15.8% / 21.3% are unweighted means of per-test rates. 3.59% and 13.63% are Python-only.
- churilov2026range: mention-level (install commands plus `ast`/tree-sitter imports with pipreqs mapping) and generation-level (≥1 hallucination per generation). One sample per prompt; live registry with a time-of-generation rule.
- krishna2025importing: per prompt (≥1 hallucinated import), N = 455 per model-language cell. Regex imports with no mapping and no stdlib filter. A date-aware definition counts post-cutoff registrations as hallucinations.
- zhao2025hfuzzer: per response (Krishna's definition), on fuzzer-optimised tasks. Names come from the model's own install-command answer (similar to Spracklen H2). Counts other-language and post-cutoff names. Not a base rate.
- haque2025secure: per Go package string; reachability oracle; about half of hallucinations in the one table shown are file paths or free text.
- zheng2026when: per source-level crate reference; 45.47% are std/module confusions; not install-level.
- dasu2026refusing: acceptance of a planted fictitious name per prompt. A different construct from spontaneous invention.
- okwor2026hallucination: no rate (distinct names and yield per generation only).
- zhang2025llm: category shares of hallucination instances only.

B. Extraction method, to record in a matrix column:
- Model-queried: Spracklen H2/H3; Zhao stage 2.
- Install-command parsing: Spracklen H1, Churilov, Haque.
- Import parsing: Churilov (pipreqs, ~1,157 names), Okwor (mapping, source unreported), Krishna (none), Zheng (crate aliases; `-`/`_` handling unreported).
- Spracklen explicitly rejects import parsing, but Churilov says it "follow[s] Spracklen's extraction approach" (p. 5). The 2024→2026 comparison is therefore not like-for-like.

C. Contradictions, for the Contradictions section (each needs data, method and time compared; any explanation labelled [I]):
1. Language.
   - Spracklen: JS > Py (unweighted means 21.3 vs 15.8, p. 7).
   - Krishna: JS lowest (14.73 vs Py 23.14, p. 8).
   - Churilov: Py > JS for every model (p. 7).
   - Candidate explanation [I]: import-based Python extraction plus module/package name mismatch, different cohorts.
2. Prompt source, same corpus.
   - Spracklen: SO > LLM-generated ([@spracklen2024we, p. 20]).
   - Churilov: LLM-generated > SO for every model ([@churilov2026range, p. 7]).
   - Same prompt sets, opposite ordering. This is the cleanest contradiction in the set.
3. Model size.
   - Krishna: larger models are better, but significance rests on n = 33 pseudo-replicates and a guessed 200B for GPT-4o.
   - Zheng: no size effect in Rust (F(1,4) = 0.0138).
   - Dasu: scale helps on impossibilities but barely on nonexistent packages.
   - Churilov: Haiku < Sonnet.
   - Zhao: Llama-3.1 > Llama-3.
4. Temperature.
   - Spracklen: rises sharply above 1 (p. 8).
   - Zheng: no effect from 0 to 2 in Rust (p. 6).
   - Zhao's temperature result is for the tester model and is not comparable.
5. Edit distance.
   - Spracklen: 13.4% within 1–2 edits and 48.6% at 6 or more (unique Python names).
   - Zheng: 40.78% within 1–2 and 86.48% within 5 (occurrence-weighted, Rust non-module).
   - Churilov: 54 of 104 universal names at distance 1.
   - Different units; do not present as a direct contradiction without saying so.
6. Cross-model overlap.
   - Spracklen: 81% of names come from a single model.
   - Churilov: mean Jaccard 0.219 and 104 universal names.
   - Okwor: 82 of 1,186 names multi-model; 450 of 455 new names single-model.
   - Zhao: 190 + 176 shared names.
   - Zheng: non-module Jaccard about 0.16.
   - Consistent picture: mostly model-specific, with a persistent shared core.
7. Mitigation effect sizes.
   - Spracklen (Python): RAG 26.28→13.40 on CodeLlama.
   - Zheng (Rust): RAG −0.34 to +1.92 points; self-refinement 2.22 to 3.26 points.
   - Same method families, very different magnitudes.

D. Registration / real-world exploitation (RQ2). These findings are compatible, not contradictory.
- Churilov: 25 of 2,282 names registered within about 6 months; 1 registered with malware; 23 suggested names with a malware history; 22 registrations not inspected.
- Okwor: 0 of 1,641 private names registered after 4 days; 22 of 149 public-list names registered, 0 malicious, 19 from one benign-placeholder operator.
- [I] Churilov's uninspected registrations may include defensive placeholders of the kind Okwor found.
- Okwor's huggingface-cli and npm examples are secondary [A] claims (p. 2).

E. Do not reuse secondary citations.
- Okwor misreports Spracklen's 21.7% as "of generations" and quotes superseded Churilov v1–3 figures (4.62–6.10% "per generation", 127 names, 53 registrable) as current. Those v1–3 rates were mention-level ([@churilov2026range, p. 6, p. 10–11]).
- Always cite the primary source.

F. Hidden quantization confound.
- Spracklen ran all open models with GPTQ (p. 6).
- Dasu ran models ≤32B at 4-bit and larger ones at full precision (p. 10).
- Zheng used Ollama models with unreported quantization.
- Haque varies quantization explicitly (Go, bitsandbytes).
- Any "size" finding involving open models may be partly a precision effect.

G. Independence and venues.
- Churilov reuses Spracklen's prompts, and earlier versions also used Spracklen's package lists, so it is not an independent prompt sample.
- Peer-reviewed: spracklen2024we (USENIX Sec '25, arXiv text analysed), zhao2025hfuzzer (ASE '25), zhang2025llm (PACMSE ISSTA '25, arXiv text analysed).
- Everything else is a preprint. okwor2026hallucination is a single-author Zenodo deposit from a company.
- No paper in this batch measures agentic tools that install dependencies automatically. That gap still needs a novelty check under §7.

Files reviewed (all under /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting/papers/<key>/): analysis.md, fulltext.txt and metadata.json for each of the nine keys.

  ### 1. liu2026packmonitor — pass-with-minor-fixes
  
  1. **Analyst notes / Source tier: validation flag not recorded.**
     - Current: nothing is said about validation.
     - Actual: `rlab validate` gives `MISMATCH`. Crossref and OpenAlex match exactly, but the arXiv title similarity is only 0.854. The PDF itself is arXiv v2, which prints the ACM DOI and "Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, ISSTA, Article ISSTA027" (p. 1).

  2. **§3 Baselines: quote is not verbatim.**
     - Current: `SR and RAG "follow prior work [41]" (p. 11)`.
     - p. 11 actually says: "Following prior work on mitigating package hallucinations [41], we include three representative baselines".
     - Fix: replace with that verbatim wording, or remove the quotation marks.
  3. **§5 Hallucination decision: wrong page for the definition.**
     - Current: "[V] a recommended package counts as hallucinated if it is not a valid PyPI name … (p. 12)".
     - p. 12 only defines the metrics. The definition is on p. 2 ("non-existent packages") and p. 6 (membership in an "official registry snapshot or a curated allowlist").
     - Fix: cite p. 2 and p. 6. Add [I]: the paper's own motivating example is an import-path vs install-name confusion ("google.protobuf" is a legitimate import path, "google-protobuf" is not a listed package; p. 6). The mask only guarantees that *some* listed name is produced.

     - Current: "It needs logits but no GPU".
     - The paper never says this. All runs were on 8×A100 (p. 12). The paper names "GPU or CPU specifications" only as a timing threat (p. 19).

[A] The authors summarise this as 'no improvement in most cases' (p. 10), which overstates the table." Update the main_finding and the evidence row to match.
  2. **§9 "Abstract ranges are not traceable" and §7 finding 1: partly wrong.**

  3. **§13 RQ4 row "Over 30% … in Odex/BigCode": overgeneralised.**

     - Fix: "≈27–30% (Odex 30.3%, BigCode 26.6%) of sampled hallucinations; authors say 'over 30%' (p. 9)."
  4. **§7 finding 2/3 and §13 row 1: detection vs correct-reason detection.**
     - The "3–85%" detection range is recall. In manual analysis, static tools were right "for the right reason" (TP) in only 37.6% (DS-1000), 4.0% (Odex) and 10.0% (BigCode) of sampled cases (Table 2, p. 8).
     - Add this to the evidence row so the matrix does not overstate detection.
  5. **§9 "Package-level results are not separated out": inaccurate.**
     - Table 3 has a "Library" cause category: 14.7 / 6.6 / 6.0% (p. 8).
     - Corrected: "Package-level causes are a small share (Library category 6–15%, p. 8); the detection metrics are not broken down by it."
  6. **Source tier: open decision.**
     - The analysis handles the TMLR claim honestly. It still needs the orchestrator to decide: re-resolve the metadata, or keep the preprint tier until the OpenReview acceptance is checked.
     - Do not hand-edit `metadata.json`.
  
  ### 7. twist2026library — pass-with-minor-fixes
  
  1. **§3 Name check and §12 "Inherit the methods": the method does not solve import names.**
     - Current: "[V] Names are compared with PyPI using PyPA name normalisation (p. 4)" and "Adopt the PyPI name normalisation".
     - p. 4 claims normalisation addresses "mismatches between import names and the registered PyPI name". PyPA normalisation only folds case and `-_.` characters; it cannot map `dateutil` → `python-dateutil` or `cv2` → `opencv-python`. The paper's own evidence shows this: the dateutil case had to be corrected manually (p. 15), and the one false positive is `pywintypes` (provided by pywin32) (p. 15).
     - Add [I]: the check effectively tests whether the import name exists on PyPI. Import names registered by third parties therefore count as valid.
     - Replace "Adopt the PyPI name normalisation" with "adopt normalisation plus an explicit import→distribution map".
  2. **§4 Sample size: unsupported.**
     - Current: "Ecosystem study: one response per task … (pp. 7, 20)".
     - p. 7 says "we then follow the same experimental setup used previously", which implies three responses. I found no statement of one response.
     - Fix: remove "one response per task", or mark it "not stated".
  3. **§5: registry lists for the other ecosystems missing.**
     - Add: JavaScript names are validated against `all-the-package-names` (jsDelivr, 2026) and Rust against the Cargo registry (p. 20). Neither snapshot is dated precisely.
     - A "January 2026 snapshot" is cited only for the top-PyPI list in the rarity study (p. 19). It does not cover the main check.
  4. **Frontmatter `main_finding`: imprecise.**
     - "user typos/fake names (up to 26%/99%)" refers to one-character typos only. Multi-character typos reach 79.44% (p. 6).
     - Fix: "one-char typos up to 26%, multi-char up to 79%, fake names up to 99%".
  
  ### 8. ohm2020backstabbers — pass-with-minor-fixes
  
  1. **Source tier: wording conflicts with §3 of the standards.**
     - Current: "LNCS book chapter … used as **background only**".
     - "Background only" is the tier-4 wording. Metadata gives a peer-reviewed proceedings chapter (`book-chapter`, Springer LNCS), which is tier 2 or better.
     - Corrected: "Tier 2 (LNCS proceedings chapter per metadata); used as background because it predates LLMs, not because of source quality."
  2. **§7 finding 5: number missing.**
     - "Most packages aim at data exfiltration" should carry the number the paper gives: 55% (p. 16–17, "(55%)" on p. 18).
  3. **§12 RQ2 placement: useful context missing.**
     - Add [V]: some typosquats have Levenshtein distance 0 because they reuse a name that exists in another repository (e.g. `python-sqlite` from apt) (p. 12).

  ---
  
  ## Cross-paper notes for the evidence matrix
  
  **A. How each paper decides that a name is hallucinated. The definitions are not comparable, so do not pool rates.**
  
  | Key | Ground truth | Snapshot date | Stdlib | Names checked | Registered-but-malicious names |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | liu2026packmonitor | PyPI list, 706,618 names via official API (p. 12, 19) | not reported | n/a (only `pip install` args) | install args after `pip install` | count as valid |
  | djire2026evaluating | registry ∪ stdlib manifests (p. 3–4) | 2026-03-04 | Python and Ruby corrected; JS/Rust unclear (p. 5) | recommended names; code-gen imports, mapping unstated | valid |
  | liu2026mitigating | on PyPI **and** ≥1 release before model cutoff (p. 5) | ~2026-06-14 (ref., p. 11); cutoffs unreported | not reported | recommendations; code-gen imports mapped by the base LLM (p. 7) | post-cutoff registrations count as hallucinated (the only paper that does this) |
  | spracklen2026llm | static PyPI snapshot (p. 20) | not reported | not reported | `pip install` lines + model answers to "required"/"useful" (p. 8) | valid; authors flag oracle poisoning (p. 12) |
  | raj2026names | live PyPI JSON API; 404 = fake, 200 → classifier (p. 5) | live, undated | not reported | import names (AST) + `pip install` in fences | **flagged** if the metadata looks suspicious |
  | mirandapena2026empirical | installed benchmark environment + builtins (p. 4, 18) | n/a | builtins allowed | imports/members at runtime | not addressed |
  | twist2026library | PyPI + PyPA normalisation (p. 4); npm list; crates (p. 20) | not reported (study Jan 2026) | not reported | import names (AST) | valid |
  
  - **Import vs install names.** raj2026names and twist2026library treat the same strings oppositely:
    - Twist counts any registered import name as valid.
    - Raj flags registered import names (`pil`, `faiss`, `skimage`) as hallucinated "squats".
    - Djire's code-generation mode and Twist probably count unregistered import names (`cv2`) as hallucinations.
    - For RQ4, record this as a contradiction caused by method, not by data.
  - **Stdlib.** Only djire2026evaluating quantifies the stdlib error (+7.6 to +9.4 pp for Python, p. 5). For the other five Python papers, base rates may carry that inflation. This is a matrix-level caveat.
  - **Release-date cutoff.** Only liu2026mitigating uses one. Every other paper scores names registered after the model's training (including attacker squats) as correct, which undercounts exploitable names. That bears directly on RQ2.
  
  **B. Hardware and access needed by each defence (RQ3/RQ5).**
  
  | Defence | Access | Hardware actually used |
  |---|---|---|
  | PackMonitor (logit masking) | white-box logits + tokenizer; no training | 8×A100 (p. 12); CPU untested |
  | Greedy / RAG / Self-Refine (djire2026evaluating) | black-box (RAG needs an index) | "single GPU", type unreported; no latency data |
  | CD / DoLa / ALCD / Nudging (djire2026evaluating) | logits or hidden states, sometimes two models | same as above |
  | BOUND (liu2026mitigating) | weights + gradients, LoRA training; adapter only at inference | 8×A100 (p. 6) |
  | Adaptive unlearning (spracklen2026llm) | full-parameter fine-tuning | MI210/MI300, 12–24 h runs (p. 8, 19) |
  | raj2026names | black-box; network calls to the PyPI JSON API + small RF/rule | API models (Groq); no local inference |
  | Static tools + grammar (mirandapena2026empirical) | CPU static analysis; grammar decoding needs local llama.cpp | M2, 24 GB RAM (p. 17); +12 s per request (p. 11) |
  | Prompting / PyPI tool (twist2026library) | black-box; the model must choose to call the tool | API only |
  | ohm2020backstabbers | user-side: pin versions, disable install scripts (p. 16) | n/a |

  - "Local" in raj2026names is the model class, not the deployment.

[41] (liu2026packmonitor p. 4, 14, 16). In the matrix, cite them to spracklen2024we, not as a replication.
  - **HFuzzer link.** liu2026mitigating shares authors with zhao2025hfuzzer, and PackMonitor uses HFuzzer as its main benchmark. These three are not independent groups.

Report absolute residual rates and the selection method next to any reduction figure.

  ### 1. liu2026packmonitor — pass-with-minor-fixes
  
  1. **Analyst notes / Source tier: validation flag not recorded.**
     - Current: nothing is said about validation.

  3. **§5 Hallucination decision: wrong page for the definition.**
     - Current: "[V] a recommended package counts as hallucinated if it is not a valid PyPI name … (p. 12)".
     - p. 12 only defines the metrics. The definition is on p. 2 ("non-existent packages") and p. 6 (membership in an "official registry snapshot or a curated allowlist").

- **Release-date cutoff.** Only liu2026mitigating uses one. Every other paper scores names registered after the model's training (including attacker squats) as correct, which undercounts exploitable names. That bears directly on RQ2.

**B. Hardware and access needed by each defence (RQ3/RQ5).**

| Defence | Access | Hardware actually used |
|---|---|---|
| PackMonitor (logit masking) | white-box logits + tokenizer; no training | 8×A100 (p. 12); CPU untested |
| Greedy / RAG / Self-Refine (djire2026evaluating) | black-box (RAG needs an index) | "single GPU", type unreported; no latency data |
| CD / DoLa / ALCD / Nudging (djire2026evaluating) | logits or hidden states, sometimes two models | same as above |
| BOUND (liu2026mitigating) | weights + gradients, LoRA training; adapter only at inference | 8×A100 (p. 6) |

Report absolute residual rates and the selection method next to any reduction figure.

  - liu2026mitigating's Qwen3 baseline of 23.29% pass@1 looks off.
  - spracklen2026llm 16B loses 7.9 pp on HumanEval.
  - Mark all utility claims as weak.
- **Persistence evidence for RQ2 is thin in this batch.** Only raj2026names reports names recurring across two same-family models (p. 10; small n, labels unaudited). Twist and Djire do not report it.

Critical-review fixes for your 4 analyses. Apply them and return the full corrected analysis.md text for all 4 keys, in the same `### FILE: papers/<key>/analysis.md` + ```markdown format as before. Do not write any files. Keep status: ready. The current versions are on disk at research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting/papers/<key>/analysis.md, so start from those.

spracklen2024we
1. §7 finding 2 and the §13 RQ1 row: the 3.59% (GPT-4 Turbo) and 13.63% (DeepSeek 1B) figures described as "overall" are the Python column of Table 7 (p. 20). JS values are GPT-4 Turbo 4.00% and DeepSeek 1B 27.45% (Table 8, p. 20). Add [I]: the paper's "overall" labels are Python-only.
2. §6/§7: add [I] that our recomputation from Tables 7–8 (p. 20) shows 5.2%, 21.7%, 15.8% and 21.3% are unweighted means of per-test rates; only 19.7% is pooled over mentions (p. 7).
3. §4 sampling: label "RQ2–RQ4 use only Python, 4 models…" as [A], and add [V] that some analyses use all 16 Python models (recency p. 8; cross-model p. 10).
4. §3 fine-tuning: the paper calls the pairs H1/H2 (pp. 12–13), but by its own definitions (pp. 6–7) they correspond to H2 (code→packages) and H3 (prompt→packages). Say so.
5. §4 data availability: change to [A] "promised" (p. 14); release confirmed by [@churilov2026range, p. 15; @churilov2026range, p. 17].
6. §5: top-k and min-p were "only tested for DeepSeek and CodeLlama" (p. 8).
7. §5/§10: add funding: UTSA FDL and NSF 2231002 (p. 14); no COI statement; findings disclosed to vendors.
8. Header: remove "according to the project lead". Tier 1 (published, USENIX Security 2025), analysed from the arXiv v3 text; venue supported by [@churilov2026range, p. 1; @churilov2026range, p. 16] and [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 9]. Metadata stays arXiv because the USENIX version has no DOI; say that in Analyst notes.

churilov2026range
1. §3/§9: "level with Spracklen's best model" compares a pooled Py+JS rate (Haiku 3.63%) with Spracklen's Python-only 3.59% [@spracklen2024we, p. 20]. Churilov's own Python-only Haiku rate is 4.38% (Table 2, p. 7). Spracklen's 5.2% and 21.7% are unweighted means of per-test rates.
2. §7 finding 2: Gemini, DeepSeek and GPT-5.4-mini are not significantly different only at the mention level; all three pairs differ at the generation level (Table 4, p. 8).
3. §7 finding 4: add [I] that the LLM-generated > SO ordering (Table 3, p. 7) reverses Spracklen's SO > LLM-generated ordering on the same corpus [@spracklen2024we, p. 20]. Record it as a contradiction.
4. §5/§10: add funding and COI from p. 15: self-funded plus a Google Cloud credit grant; "no conflicts of interest"; Claude used for analysis code and drafting.
5. §4: add [V] that the released corpus has 39,969 prompts (20,163 SO + 19,806 LLM) (p. 4). Add [I] that this does not match Spracklen's stated 2×19,200 (p. 6) or 19,500 (p. 2).

okwor2026hallucination
1. Header: `rlab validate` gives MISMATCH because Crossref has no record (it is a DataCite DOI) while OpenAlex matches. Resolved on 2026-11-12 via the Zenodo API: 10.5281/zenodo.21199426 is the concept DOI and …427 (printed on p. 1) is the version DOI of the same deposit. State this in the header or Analyst notes.
2. §7 finding 7 (npm mirror unreliable): change to [A] (p. 3), partly supported by the 11 negative-control names that predate t0 and were missed by the mirror [V] (p. 7).
3. §7 finding 4 (19 placeholders from one operator): change to [A], evidence withheld (p. 6). Only the shared summary string is [V] (p. 5).
4. §7 finding 5: give the scope. Of the 2,000 extra generations, 11 names were absent from the snapshot but live (p. 7); the author calls this "essentially uninformative" (p. 7).
5. Add a secondary [A] claim citing grey sources (p. 2), not verified by this paper: huggingface-cli drew more than 30,000 downloads in 3 months, and an npm name spread to 237 GitHub repositories before being defensively claimed.
6. §5 code availability: change to [A] promised (p. 8); we did not check whether the deposit exists.
7. Tier: justify the choice. It is self-labelled "Preprint" (p. 1); single author, company-affiliated, Zenodo self-deposit, no peer review. Tier 3 or 4 is fine as long as the reason is stated.

krishna2025importing
1. §10: it is not the only Rust study. Change to "[V] covers Rust/crates.io alongside JS and Python (p. 4). [I] Within the project, Rust is also covered by [@zheng2026when] and [@dasu2026refusing]."
2. §4: add [I] that the Table 3 values are multiples of 1/455, which supports N = 455 per model-language cell (p. 4). Nemotron's 0.22% is a single prompt.
3. §9: add [I] that the size correlation depends on an unverified 200B estimate for GPT-4o (Table 1 footnote, p. 3).
4. §7 finding 3: add that the lowest Python value is Dracarys at 2.42% (Table 3, p. 4; p. 5).

  ### 1. liu2026packmonitor — pass-with-minor-fixes

  3. **§5 Hallucination decision: wrong page for the definition.**
     - Current: "[V] a recommended package counts as hallucinated if it is not a valid PyPI name … (p. 12)".

     - Current: "It needs logits but no GPU".
     - The paper never says this. All runs were on 8×A100 (p. 12). The paper names "GPU or CPU specifications" only as a timing threat (p. 19).
     - Fix: "[I] Needs a locally decoded open-weight model exposing logits and its tokenizer. CPU-only operation is untested; all timings come from an A100 server (p. 12, p. 19). DFA loading of ≤0.25 s (p. 17) is a host-side cost and does not show the 7–8B decoding itself is laptop-feasible."
  5. **§7 finding 1: fair comparison context missing.**
     - The "best baseline" RAG+SR on CodeLlama (1.30% PHR) comes with only 231 recommended packages, against 1,004 for vanilla (p. 13).
     - Add this clause here as well as in §9, so the evidence matrix does not cite 1.30% as a like-for-like rate.
  
  ### 2. djire2026evaluating — pass-with-minor-fixes
  
  1. **§9 Internal inconsistencies, third bullet: wrong accusation.**
     - Current: "The conclusion says CD 'reduced hallucination in 19 of 32' … The results say CD is never lowest".
     - These two statements measure different things, and both are true:
       - From Table 4 (p. 7), CD is below Vanilla in exactly 19/32 cells: gemma-1b 4, gemma-4b 2, llama-8b 4, mistral 2, qwen-1.5b 4, qwen-3b 3, deepseek 0.
       - CD is the lowest strategy in no cell (p. 6).
     - The Nudging point is also misquoted. The conclusion gives Nudging the best trade-off "among the guided decoding strategies", and in the same paragraph says "Greedy decoding provides the strongest average trade-off, followed by Self-Refine and Nudging" (p. 11).

  2. **§9 first bullet: "18 of 32" mis-framed.**

  3. **New §9 item: author claim contradicted by the paper's own table.**

  4. **§3 Nudging: unexplained surrogate design.**
     - Current: "[V] Nudging: the surrogate is the largest model in the family".

  5. **§4 Sample: wrong unit.**
     - Current: "Generated packages per configuration range from 1,470 to 32,337 (Table 3, p. 6)".
     - Table 3 covers vanilla decoding only, per model × language.

  6. **§13 Evidence table, RQ3 "Guided decoding … needs internal access" row: labels mixed.**
     - The row is labelled V but mixes our [I] about access with [V] results.
     - Fix: split it into a V row (DoLa 38.0% average; syntax errors) and an I row (white-box access needed).
     - The RQ5 row "Latency/overhead … not reported" is labelled A, but it is our observation. Relabel it I.
  7. **§5: import→distribution mapping consequence missing.**

     - Add [I]: in the code-generation extension, imports are "validated against the same registry snapshots" (p. 6). Unregistered import names such as `cv2` therefore probably count as hallucinations, which inflates the code-generation counts in Fig. 1.
  
  ### 3. liu2026mitigating — pass-with-minor-fixes

     - Table II (p. 7): Valid-Rate rises +6.4% on edit prompts. On unseen prompts Qwen3 falls 0.7990 → 0.7434 (−7.0%) and DeepSeekCoder rises 0.7978 → 0.8909. Only HumanEval stays within ±2% (Table VI, p. 9).
     - Corrected: "…Valid-Rate rises on average (+6.4% edit) but falls 7% for Qwen3 on unseen prompts; HumanEval within ±2%."
  2. **§13 cost row: unit not supported.**
     - Current: "editing ~83 s + localization ~24 s per model".
     - Table V gives averages "across models" and does not define the unit (per fold of 50 edit cases is likely) (p. 9).

  3. **§5 cost table: cheaper baselines omitted.**

     - So the paper's statement that BOUND's editing "is lower than ROME, MEMIT, and Full-FT" is true only because DINM is left out.
     - Add these rows, or a note.

     - On DeepSeekCoder Edit50, Full-FT beats BOUND: Package-HR 0.0188 vs 0.0745, Valid-Rate 0.9500 vs 0.9480 (Table II, p. 7).

  ### 5. raj2026names — pass-with-minor-fixes
  
  1. **Source tier / Analyst notes: verification status misstated.**
     - Current: "`metadata.json` verification is 'single-source (openalex)'" and "Verification is single-source".

     - Corrected: "rlab validate: MISMATCH (arXiv and OpenAlex agree; the Zenodo DOI is not in Crossref); PDF identity probable."
  2. **§5 / §9: standard-library (stdlib) handling not reported.**
     - The extractor keeps every top-level import module from the AST (p. 5), and any PyPI 404 is "fake" (p. 5). Without a stdlib filter, `import os`/`json`/`sys` would trigger retries.
     - The paper never says how stdlib modules are excluded. A grep finds no "stdlib", "standard library" or "built-in".
     - Add "Stdlib handling: not reported", plus [I] that this directly affects give-up rates.
  3. **§7 finding 4 [I]: stronger evidence available from the paper itself.**

     - The 404 half also contains import-name errors: `pkg-resources` (the module `pkg_resources` ships with setuptools) is listed as an invention (p. 8). The paper also counts `faiss` as a "hallucinatory variant" in the bait test (p. 11).

  4. **§13 RQ4 row "fixing extraction … cut give-up from 79% to ~29%": strength too high.**
     - Currently V / moderate. The versions were run on different, overlapping prompt sets (70, 58, 60 and 300 prompts; Table 1, p. 7) with no fixed comparison set.
     - Change strength to weak, and add "different prompt sets".
  5. **§9 (optional): factual error in the paper's related work.**
     - Add [I]: the paper attributes the term "slopsquatting" to Spracklen et al. (2024) (p. 2). The paper gives no evidence for this attribution.
     - Its 3-item reference list (p. 15) supports the weak-grounding point.

  1. **§7 finding 6, §13 RQ3 row 3, frontmatter `main_finding`, §12: wrong RIF claim.**
     - Current: "The RIF does not fall and increases on Odex" / "does not reduce the hallucination share (RIF)" / "LLM repair improves execution, not hallucinations".
     - Table 5 (p. 10) shows RIF falls sharply on DS-1000 for every model and every repair method, e.g. claude-3 9.1 → 2.7, Gemma2 22.3 → 8.1, Qwen3 25.4 → 6.1. It rises on Odex for the small models, and is roughly flat on BigCode.
     - The analysis repeats the authors' "In most cases, there is no improvement in fixing hallucinations" (p. 10) as [V], but their own table contradicts it.
     - Corrected: "[V] RIF falls on DS-1000 for all models (e.g. 9.1 → 2.7), is roughly flat on BigCode, and rises on Odex for the small models (e.g. Qwen3 31.3 → 55.6) (p. 10). [A] The authors summarise this as 'no improvement in most cases' (p. 10), which overstates the table." Update the main_finding and the evidence row to match.
  2. **§9 "Abstract ranges are not traceable" and §7 finding 1: partly wrong.**
     - The abstract's "14-85% of library hallucinations" is exactly Pyright's IFR range in Table 10 (0.14–0.85, p. 20).
     - Correct the bullet: "14–85% = Pyright IFR range (p. 20). '16–70%' and '8.1–40%' could not be matched (Pyright all-error recall is 0.16–0.82, p. 6; no-repair RIF is 8.1–44.9, p. 10)."
  3. **§13 RQ4 row "Over 30% … in Odex/BigCode": overgeneralised.**
     - "Ambiguous output" is 30.3% on Odex but 26.6% on BigCode (Table 3, p. 8).
     - Fix: "≈27–30% (Odex 30.3%, BigCode 26.6%) of sampled hallucinations; authors say 'over 30%' (p. 9)."
  4. **§7 finding 2/3 and §13 row 1: detection vs correct-reason detection.**
     - The "3–85%" detection range is recall. In manual analysis, static tools were right "for the right reason" (TP) in only 37.6% (DS-1000), 4.0% (Odex) and 10.0% (BigCode) of sampled cases (Table 2, p. 8).
     - Add this to the evidence row so the matrix does not overstate detection.
  5. **§9 "Package-level results are not separated out": inaccurate.**
     - Table 3 has a "Library" cause category: 14.7 / 6.6 / 6.0% (p. 8).
     - Corrected: "Package-level causes are a small share (Library category 6–15%, p. 8); the detection metrics are not broken down by it."
  6. **Source tier: open decision.**
     - The analysis handles the TMLR claim honestly. It still needs the orchestrator to decide: re-resolve the metadata, or keep the preprint tier until the OpenReview acceptance is checked.
     - Do not hand-edit `metadata.json`.

     - Current: "[V] Names are compared with PyPI using PyPA name normalisation (p. 4)" and "Adopt the PyPI name normalisation".
     - p. 4 claims normalisation addresses "mismatches between import names and the registered PyPI name". PyPA normalisation only folds case and `-_.` characters; it cannot map `dateutil` → `python-dateutil` or `cv2` → `opencv-python`. The paper's own evidence shows this: the dateutil case had to be corrected manually (p. 15), and the one false positive is `pywintypes` (provided by pywin32) (p. 15).
     - Add [I]: the check effectively tests whether the import name exists on PyPI. Import names registered by third parties therefore count as valid.
     - Replace "Adopt the PyPI name normalisation" with "adopt normalisation plus an explicit import→distribution map".
  2. **§4 Sample size: unsupported.**
     - Current: "Ecosystem study: one response per task … (pp. 7, 20)".
     - p. 7 says "we then follow the same experimental setup used previously", which implies three responses. I found no statement of one response.
     - Fix: remove "one response per task", or mark it "not stated".
  3. **§5: registry lists for the other ecosystems missing.**
     - Add: JavaScript names are validated against `all-the-package-names` (jsDelivr, 2026) and Rust against the Cargo registry (p. 20). Neither snapshot is dated precisely.
     - A "January 2026 snapshot" is cited only for the top-PyPI list in the rarity study (p. 19). It does not cover the main check.
  4. **Frontmatter `main_finding`: imprecise.**
     - "user typos/fake names (up to 26%/99%)" refers to one-character typos only. Multi-character typos reach 79.44% (p. 6).

  | djire2026evaluating | registry ∪ stdlib manifests (p. 3–4) | 2026-03-04 | Python and Ruby corrected; JS/Rust unclear (p. 5) | recommended names; code-gen imports, mapping unstated | valid |
  | liu2026mitigating | on PyPI **and** ≥1 release before model cutoff (p. 5) | ~2026-06-14 (ref., p. 11); cutoffs unreported | not reported | recommendations; code-gen imports mapped by the base LLM (p. 7) | post-cutoff registrations count as hallucinated (the only paper that does this) |
  | spracklen2026llm | static PyPI snapshot (p. 20) | not reported | not reported | `pip install` lines + model answers to "required"/"useful" (p. 8) | valid; authors flag oracle poisoning (p. 12) |
  | raj2026names | live PyPI JSON API; 404 = fake, 200 → classifier (p. 5) | live, undated | not reported | import names (AST) + `pip install` in fences | **flagged** if the metadata looks suspicious |
  | mirandapena2026empirical | installed benchmark environment + builtins (p. 4, 18) | n/a | builtins allowed | imports/members at runtime | not addressed |
  | twist2026library | PyPI + PyPA normalisation (p. 4); npm list; crates (p. 20) | not reported (study Jan 2026) | not reported | import names (AST) | valid |
  
  - **Import vs install names.** raj2026names and twist2026library treat the same strings oppositely:
    - Twist counts any registered import name as valid.
    - Raj flags registered import names (`pil`, `faiss`, `skimage`) as hallucinated "squats".
    - Djire's code-generation mode and Twist probably count unregistered import names (`cv2`) as hallucinations.
    - For RQ4, record this as a contradiction caused by method, not by data.
  - **Stdlib.** Only djire2026evaluating quantifies the stdlib error (+7.6 to +9.4 pp for Python, p. 5). For the other five Python papers, base rates may carry that inflation. This is a matrix-level caveat.
  - **Release-date cutoff.** Only liu2026mitigating uses one. Every other paper scores names registered after the model's training (including attacker squats) as correct, which undercounts exploitable names. That bears directly on RQ2.
  
  **B. Hardware and access needed by each defence (RQ3/RQ5).**
  
  | Defence | Access | Hardware actually used |
  |---|---|---|
  | PackMonitor (logit masking) | white-box logits + tokenizer; no training | 8×A100 (p. 12); CPU untested |
  | Greedy / RAG / Self-Refine (djire2026evaluating) | black-box (RAG needs an index) | "single GPU", type unreported; no latency data |
  | CD / DoLa / ALCD / Nudging (djire2026evaluating) | logits or hidden states, sometimes two models | same as above |
  | BOUND (liu2026mitigating) | weights + gradients, LoRA training; adapter only at inference | 8×A100 (p. 6) |
  | Adaptive unlearning (spracklen2026llm) | full-parameter fine-tuning | MI210/MI300, 12–24 h runs (p. 8, 19) |
  | raj2026names | black-box; network calls to the PyPI JSON API + small RF/rule | API models (Groq); no local inference |
  | Static tools + grammar (mirandapena2026empirical) | CPU static analysis; grammar decoding needs local llama.cpp | M2, 24 GB RAM (p. 17); +12 s per request (p. 11) |
  | Prompting / PyPI tool (twist2026library) | black-box; the model must choose to call the tool | API only |
  | ohm2020backstabbers | user-side: pin versions, disable install scripts (p. 16) | n/a |
  
  - Only mirandapena2026empirical actually ran on a laptop-class machine.
  - "Local" in raj2026names is the model class, not the deployment.
  
  **C. Contradictions and duplicated data.**
  
  - **SFT numbers are not independent.** PackMonitor's Package4U vanilla and SFT figures (16.14 / 26.28 → 2.66 / 10.27%) and the HumanEval drops (−26.9 / −14.0) are quoted from Spracklen et al. [41] (liu2026packmonitor p. 4, 14, 16). In the matrix, cite them to spracklen2024we, not as a replication.
  - **HFuzzer link.** liu2026mitigating shares authors with zhao2025hfuzzer, and PackMonitor uses HFuzzer as its main benchmark. These three are not independent groups.

That is a typosquat-amplification threat, not spontaneous invention, and the metrics differ.
  - **Relative vs absolute reductions.** liu2026mitigating (−65.4%) and spracklen2026llm (−88%) report relative reductions on deliberately hallucination-heavy prompt sets (selected for Sample-HR > 0.5, or hand-picked). twist2026library shows near-0% under ordinary prompts (p. 5). Report absolute residual rates and the selection method next to any reduction figure.
  - **Utility evidence is weak everywhere.**
    - PackMonitor's HumanEval check cannot trigger the intervention (no `pip install` in HumanEval).
    - liu2026mitigating's Qwen3 baseline of 23.29% pass@1 looks off.
    - spracklen2026llm 16B loses 7.9 pp on HumanEval.
    - Mark all utility claims as weak.

Critical review of the 17 analyses is done. Both reports are in [reports/](research/2026-11-12-package-hallucination-and-slopsquatting/reports/).

- **Result:** 15 analyses need only minor fixes, and 2 needed bigger corrections. The Okwor paper's DOI question is resolved (both DOIs point to the same paper). The mirandapena2026empirical analysis had the repair result wrong against the paper's table, and that has now been sent back for correction.
- **Fixes in progress:** all 4 analyst agents have their corrections and are applying them. When the corrected versions come back, I'll save them, re-check the citations and mark them complete.

**Notable cross-paper findings:**
- **Rates can't be compared directly.** Each paper decides "hallucinated" differently: by package name or by import name, with or without filtering out standard-library modules, and against different registry snapshots. That's why some papers find JS higher than Python and others find the reverse.
- **No defence has been shown on an ordinary laptop.** PackMonitor and BOUND ran on 8×A100 GPUs, and unlearning needs a full fine-tune. Only the static-analysis study ran on a laptop-class Mac M2.
- **A gap that fits you well:** a cheap check that runs on the user's side, on a laptop, against the live registry, and handles import names versus install names properly (cv2 → opencv-python). There is a method contradiction here that nobody has resolved yet. The novelty check will confirm whether this gap really exists.

I still need your decision on the 3 attack papers: should I use only their abstracts?

---
name: compare-methods
description: Compare methodologies, datasets, metrics and findings across a project's analysed papers, consolidate the evidence matrix and identify contradictions. Use after paper analyses are complete, or when the user asks how studies differ or agree.
---

# Compare methodologies

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §1, §5, §6.

Input: project id. Use only analyses with `status: ready` or `complete`; `rlab index <id>` then read `literature-matrix.md` for the overview, and each `papers/*/analysis.md` for detail.

## 1. Evidence matrix
Merge every analysis's evidence table (section 13) into `evidence-matrix.md`, one row per claim, Source as `[@key, p. N]`. Keep the paper's label; downgrade strength for abstract-only and preprint sources.

## 2. Methodology comparison
Write `reports/methodology-comparison.md`:
1. **Overview table** — one row per paper: design, data/sample (N), setup, metrics, baselines, statistical testing, reproducibility (data/code available).
2. **Approach families** — group papers by method; for each group: typical strengths, weaknesses, and which papers [@key].
3. **Comparable results** — compare numbers only between papers sharing dataset, metric and setup; say explicitly when results are not comparable and why.
4. **Contradictions** — copy to `evidence-matrix.md` "Contradictions": claims, sources, differences in data/population/method/metric/time, possible explanation labelled [I].
5. **Methodological weaknesses across the field** — recurring problems (small N, no baselines, no significance tests, leakage risk, no code). These feed gap finding.
6. **What this means for our RQs** — per RQ, current answer with evidence strength; update "Current answer" in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

## 3. Check
`rlab cite-check <id> research/<id>/evidence-matrix.md research/<id>/reports/methodology-comparison.md` passes.

Done when: every ready/complete paper appears in the overview table, every RQ has a current answer with strength, cite-check passes. Tick Synthesis in `STATUS.md`.
# Evidence matrix — Package Hallucination and Slopsquatting in LLM Coding Assistants: Measuring Hallucinated Dependencies, Their Exploitability on PyPI/npm, and Lightweight Defences

One row per piece of evidence that bears on a research question. Source is `[@key, p. N]` (checked by `rlab cite-check`).
Label: **VERIFIED** (checked in the paper's own data/results), **AUTHOR-CLAIM** (stated by authors, not independently checkable), **INTERPRETATION** (our reasoning).
Strength: strong / moderate / weak (see docs/research-standards.md).

| RQ | Claim / finding | Source | Label | Design & N | Strength | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

# Merge §13 evidence tables of complete analyses into evidence-matrix.md rows (stdout).
import re, sys, json, pathlib
proj = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
DOWN = {'strong': 'moderate', 'moderate': 'weak', 'weak': 'weak'}
def cite(key, pages):
    parts = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r'[,;]', pages) if re.search(r'\d', p)]
    if not parts: return f'[@{key}]'
    return '[' + '; '.join(f"@{key}, {'pp.' if re.search(r'[–-]', p) else 'p.'} {p.replace('p.','').strip()}" for p in parts) + ']'
rows = []
for d in sorted((proj / 'papers').iterdir()):
    a = (d / 'analysis.md').read_text()
    if not re.search(r'^status: complete$', a, re.M): continue
    meta = json.loads((d / 'metadata.json').read_text())
    pre = meta.get('venue_kind') == 'preprint'
    ss = re.search(r'^sample_size: (.*)$', a, re.M)
    design = (ss.group(1).strip() if ss else '')[:90].replace('|', '/')
    sec = re.search(r'^## 13\..*?\n(.*?)(?=^## 14\.)', a, re.M | re.S).group(1)
    for line in sec.splitlines():
        c = [x.strip() for x in line.strip().strip('|').split('|')]
        if len(c) < 5 or not c[0].upper().startswith('RQ') : continue
        rq, claim, page, label, strength = c[0], c[1], c[2], c[3], c[4].lower()
        label = re.sub(r'^\[?([VAI])\]?', r'[\1]', label)
        base = strength.split()[0] if strength and strength[0].isalpha() else strength
        st = DOWN.get(base, strength) if pre and base in DOWN else strength
        note = 'preprint (strength downgraded)' if pre and base in ('strong', 'moderate') else ('preprint' if pre else '')
        rows.append(f'| {rq} | {claim} | {cite(d.name, page)} | {label} | {design} | {st} | {note} |')
print('\n'.join(rows)); print(len(rows), 'rows', file=sys.stderr)
EOF

[I] Import parsing over-counts Python module names that differ from distribution names (cv2, sklearn), which plausibly explains much of the reversal.
2. **Prompt source on the same corpus (RQ1/RQ4).** Stack Overflow prompts > LLM-generated prompts for almost every model in [@spracklen2024we, p. 20]; LLM-generated > Stack Overflow for every model in [@churilov2026range, p. 7]. Same released prompt corpus, different models, extraction and time (2024 vs 2026). [I] Cleanest contradiction in the set; cause unresolved.
3. **Model size (RQ1).** Larger models hallucinate less in [@krishna2025importing, p. 6] (r = −0.542, but 33 pseudo-replicated points and an estimated 200B GPT-4o size, [@krishna2025importing, p. 3]); no size effect for Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 6]; newer Llama-3.1-8B produced more unique hallucinated names than Llama-3-8B in [@zhao2025hfuzzer, p. 7]. [I] Size is confounded with quantization (GPTQ for all open models in [@spracklen2024we, p. 6]; 4-bit ≤32B in [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10]; explicit quantization effects in [@haque2025secure, p. 6]).
4. **Temperature (RQ1).** Rates rise sharply above temperature 1 in [@spracklen2024we, p. 8]; no effect from 0 to 2 for Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 6]. Different ecosystem and extraction; not resolved.
5. **Import names: valid or hallucinated? (RQ4).** [@twist2026library, p. 4] counts any import name registered on PyPI as valid (PyPA normalisation only, [@twist2026library, p. 15]); [@raj2026names, p. 8] flags registered import names such as pil and faiss as squats; [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6] validates code-generation imports against the registry, so unregistered import names (cv2) probably count as hallucinations. [I] Method-driven contradiction: the field has no shared import→distribution mapping.

[I] RAG is ecosystem- and retriever-dependent and not a reliable defence on its own.
7. **Real-world registration (RQ2) — compatible, not contradictory.** 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names registered within about six months, one with malware [@churilov2026range, p. 12]; 0 of 1,641 private names registered after 4 days and 22 of 149 public names registered, none malicious, 19 defensive placeholders [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 5]. Different windows and sampling frames.

## Agreements / converging evidence

- Every study that measures it finds non-zero package hallucination in all tested models, from 2023–24 open models ([@spracklen2024we, p. 7]) to 2026 frontier models ([@churilov2026range, p. 6]), and in Rust and Go as well as Python/JS ([@zheng2026when, p. 5]; [@haque2025secure, p. 6]).
- Hallucinated names are mostly model-specific with a persistent shared core: 81% single-model names in [@spracklen2024we, p. 10]; 104 names shared by all five 2026 models in [@churilov2026range, p. 9]; 450 of 455 new names single-model in [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 4]. Many recur across re-runs (43% in 10/10 runs, [@spracklen2024we, p. 9]).
- Registry existence checks are necessary but not sufficient: registered lookalikes and import-name collisions pass a plain 200/404 check ([@raj2026names, p. 8]; [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 6]; [@spracklen2024we, p. 12]).
- White-box defences (logit masking, model editing, unlearning) reach large reductions but need weights or logits and GPU servers ([@liu2026packmonitor, p. 12]; [@liu2026mitigating, p. 6]; [@spracklen2026llm, p. 8]); only static analysis ran on a laptop-class machine ([@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 17]).
- Models largely accept user-supplied fake package names (compliance, not invention): [@djire2026evaluating, p. 9]; [@twist2026library, p. 6]; [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
'''
a=s.index('## Contradictions')
s=s[:a]+con
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

verification and updating. We refer to these types of filtering

        - one cheap frontier API model from Churilov's cohort (e.g., Claude Haiku 4.5 or GPT-5.4-mini);
        - one local model (qwen2.5-coder:7b, Ollama default quantization).
      - Tasks:
        - 200 Python tasks (optionally 100 JavaScript tasks) phrased neutrally ("Write and run a script that … Install whatever you need.");
        - converted from the public prompt corpus released with Spracklen/Churilov (39,969 prompts, [@churilov2026range, p. 4]);
        - stratified by Stack Overflow vs LLM-generated source and by topic recency, because both shift rates [@churilov2026range, p. 7; @spracklen2024we, pp. 8–9].
        - No fake names and no adversarial text in prompts.
      - 3 runs per task × agent × model (persistence).
      - **Baseline:** the same model in single-turn chat on the same task, scored with the same protocol.
    - **Metrics:**
      1. Per-task install-attempt hallucination rate: at least one install request for a name absent from the registry at run time. Report Wilson 95% CIs. With 0 events, use the rule-of-three upper bound.
      2. Per-install-command rate.
      3. Category shares: non-existent / import-name used as install name (e.g., `pip install cv2`) / registered lookalike / registered after model cutoff / correct.
      4. Post-404 behaviour distribution, including whether a substitute name is itself a low-reputation lookalike.
      5. Run-to-run persistence and Jaccard overlap of names across agents.
    - **Analysis:**
      - Paired agent-vs-chat comparison per task (McNemar);
      - logistic mixed model with a task random effect (agent, model, ecosystem, prompt source as fixed effects);
      - pre-register hypotheses and stopping rules.
    - **Sample-size reasoning:** if the true per-task rate is about 3%, 600 runs per configuration give about 18 events, a CI of roughly ±1.4 pp. Zero events bounds the rate below 0.5%, which is itself a publishable result.
    - **Cost and time:**
      - API agent runs use about 20k–100k tokens each, roughly $0.05–0.50 per run with a small model. Cap the API arm at 100 tasks × 3 runs, about ≤ $100.
      - Local Ollama arm: free, about 2–5 min per run on Apple Silicon, so about 20–50 h unattended.
      - Total 4–6 weeks.
    - **Expected threats to validity:**
      - low base rate (power);
      - proxy blocking alters downstream behaviour (mitigate: return a byte-identical registry 404);
      - agent and model version drift (log versions and dates);
      - task-selection bias towards install-heavy tasks [I], the same bias noted for Haque's GPT-4o filtering;
      - import-name ambiguity (handled by G3).
  
  - **Feasibility for a beginner: moderate.**
    - Docker, a proxy and agent CLIs are well documented, and all scoring is offline Python.
    - The hard part is safe sandboxing and enough runs to get events. Phase 0 gives a no-risk start.

  - **Gap type:** practical + methodological.

    - Existence checks are necessary but not sufficient (stated by several papers):
      - [A] Plain registry checks are inadequate because attackers can pre-register names [@spracklen2024we, p. 12].
      - [I] Any registry-present name passes PackMonitor's mask, and vetted allowlists are not evaluated [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 6; @liu2026packmonitor, p. 19].
      - [A] If attackers pre-register hallucinated names, a registry oracle labels them valid (oracle poisoning) [@spracklen2026llm, p. 12].
    - The hard cases are real:
      - [V] 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names were registered within about six months, and at least 23 suggested names previously hosted malware [@churilov2026range, p. 12].
      - [V] 19 of 22 registered public names are placeholders [@okwor2026hallucination, pp. 5–6], and [A] a placeholder can be weaponised in a later release [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 8].
      - [V] Import names of real packages were the largest false-positive class (144–207 mentions per model) [@churilov2026range, p. 10].
    - Proposed but **not evaluated** defences:
      - [A] a date-aware verification list [@krishna2025importing, p. 8];
      - [A] registry grounding at generation time [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9];
      - [A] guided decoding plus lightweight registry verification [@djire2026evaluating, p. 11];
      - [A] a namespace- and near-miss-aware Rust guardrail [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
    - The only black-box guard in the set has known false-positive and drift problems:
      - [A] Its top feature (maintainers) is about 0 through the PyPI JSON API, risking false positives on small or new legitimate packages [@raj2026names, p. 13].

      - [V] Half of its "registered lookalike" flags are the import names `pil`/`faiss` [@raj2026names, p. 8].
    - Forced versus optional checks: [V] a model-callable existence tool is rarely called by GPT-5-mini [@twist2026library, p. 8]. [I] This supports a *forced* client-side check over a tool the model may skip.

  ## G3: There is no validated, shared protocol for deciding whether an LLM-mentioned package is hallucinated, and the analysed papers' rules disagree enough to change conclusions
  
  - **Gap type:** methodological + contradiction.
  
  - **Evidence that the gap exists:**
    - **Import names (contradiction 5 in the evidence matrix):**
      - [V] Twist counts any registered import name as valid, with PyPA normalisation only [@twist2026library, p. 4; @twist2026library, p. 15].
      - [V] Raj flags registered import names (`pil`, `faiss`) as squats [@raj2026names, p. 8].
      - [I] Djire validates code-generation imports against the registry without a reported mapping, so `cv2`-type names probably count as hallucinations [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6].
    - **Extraction:**
      - [A] Spracklen rejects import parsing because module names do not map to package names [@spracklen2024we, p. 6].
      - [I] Churilov claims to follow Spracklen yet parses imports [@churilov2026range, p. 5].
      - [V] 34 of 46 GPT-4o hallucinations in HFuzzer are install-name errors with a correct import [@zhao2025hfuzzer, p. 9].
    - **Stdlib:** [V] treating stdlib modules as hallucinations inflates Python PHR by +7.6 to +9.4 pp [@djire2026evaluating, p. 5]. [V] Raj does not report stdlib handling [@raj2026names, p. 5].
    - **Snapshots and time:**
      - [V] Static lists miscounted and inflated rates by about 1/5 compared with live two-round validation [@churilov2026range, p. 10].
      - [V] Only two papers apply a release-date or cutoff rule [@krishna2025importing, p. 3; @liu2026mitigating, p. 5].
      - [A] The public npm name mirror is unreliable [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 3].
    - **Units:** [V] per-prompt [@krishna2025importing, p. 4] vs per-mention [@spracklen2024we, p. 7] vs per-string including file paths [@haque2025secure, p. 8] vs per source-level crate reference, including std-module confusions [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
    - **Extractor errors dominate small studies:** [V] most early "hallucinations" were extractor false positives [@raj2026names, p. 7].
    - **The contradictions may be method artefacts:**
      - [V] Language direction: JS > Py in Spracklen [@spracklen2024we, p. 7] vs Py > JS in Krishna and Churilov [@krishna2025importing, p. 8; @churilov2026range, p. 7].
      - [V] Prompt-source ordering reverses on the *same* corpus [@spracklen2024we, p. 20; @churilov2026range, p. 7].
      - [I] Both are plausibly driven by extraction and import-name handling. Untested.
    - Independent support: six or more papers from different groups use incompatible rules, and the critical reviews flagged it as the field's main comparability problem.
  
  - **Novelty check (2026-11-12):**
    - `rlab search` queries (Crossref + arXiv, 2024–):
      1. `import name distribution name mapping Python package` — Crossref 24; nothing relevant.
      2. `package hallucination measurement methodology registry snapshot` — Crossref 24; only djire2026evaluating (in project).
      3. `package hallucination benchmark standardized evaluation` — Crossref 17, arXiv 1; general hallucination benchmarks only.
      4. `hallucinated imports registry` — arXiv 3.
      5. Plus the shared sweeps.
    - WebSearch: one query on an import vs install name measurement protocol. It found "no standardized protocol", only per-paper reconcilers and tool alias tables (e.g., pkghall's ~180-alias table, Socket's glossary examples).
    - Closest:
      - churilov2026range's live two-round protocol (in project; the most complete, but its pipreqs map covers only about 1,157 import names, [@churilov2026range, p. 14], and it is unvalidated against human labels);
      - Hillah et al. (arXiv 2606.13918; calibration of one detector, not a cross-rule protocol);
      - Al-Zofi systematic review (Research Square 2025, 10.21203/rs.3.rs-8007192/v1; synthesises definitions, no protocol validation).
    - Result: we found no study that re-scores the same generations under the different published decision rules, validates them against human labels, and tests whether the documented contradictions survive (searches on 2026-11-12).
  
  - **Confidence: medium-high.**

    - Against: the risk is that a methodology note gets less attention than an attack or defence paper.
  
  - **Potential contribution:**

    - an open reference scorer (a small pip-installable library);
    - a human-labelled gold set;
